#7770. ‘ER’ and ‘The Pitt’ are similar enough for lawsuit to move forward, appeals court says

Actor Noah Wyle attends an event for HBO’s “The Pitt” at the David Geffen Theater on June 9, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Photo by Phillip Faraone/Getty Images for HBO)

A unanimous California appeals court on Wednesday found that medical TV shows ER and The Pitt have enough similarities that a lawsuit alleging that The Pitt is an unauthorized rebranded version of ER can move forward.

A three-judge panel from the Second District Court of Appeal in California ruled that the trial court judge correctly rejected a motion to dismiss the case brought by the widow and estate of ER creator Michael Crichton.

However, the panel dismissed actor Noah Wyle, who starred in both shows and produces The Pitt, as a defendant, along with two other producers who worked on both series.

The Pitt is an HBO Max series depicting a real-time day in the life of a Pittsburgh emergency department. It has won two Emmy Awards for best drama for its first two seasons and two Emmy Awards for Wyle for best actor, according to a story by the Associated Press.

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Hydroponic systems, which allow plants to grow in water rather than soil, are popular because they offer a way to produce a bounty of plants in a relatively small area in an indoor garden. These systems also tend to be user-friendly, so even newbie growers are likely to succeed. We recently tested eight popular models, spending several months setting them up and evaluating their various features while growing a range of plants.

We also evaluated each tested hydroponics system for its ease of use, value, functionality, appearance, and build quality. With these factors in mind, our favorite is Ahopegarden’s 10-Pod Aeroponics Growing Kit. It offers the flexibility to grow almost any type of plant, is easy to set up, and provides a good value for the money.

But Ahopegarden isn’t the only show in town. Some of the other kits we tested also ranked highly and may better fit your indoor gardening needs depending on the available space and desired setup. Check out our top picks of some of the best hydroponic systems to get started.

Bottom line: Explore the best hydroponic systems of 2026, from compact kits to large setups, each offering unique features for indoor gardening success.

To qualify as one of our top picks, we required each hydroponic system to have a water circulation system to keep the water fresh. When evaluating all-inclusive systems, we looked for bright grow lights that could be adjusted in height as the plants grow taller. The following hydroponic systems vary in design and size, but each is well suited to growing healthy herbs and plants indoors.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 5/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 5/5

The Ahopegarden offers an affordable way to grow fruits, vegetables, or flowers at home. It has the capacity to grow 10 plants and comes with baskets, sponges, plant food, and grow domes—everything needed to get started except for seeds. While this system can be used to produce any type of plant, the adjustable light reaches a maximum height of 14.6 inches, so users will need to select plant varieties that won’t exceed this.

We chose a dwarf tomato variety and mini bell pepper to grow in our Ahopegarden, planting five of each seed. Setting the system up required us to soak the sponges, fill the water tank, and use tweezers to add 2 to 3 seeds to each sponge (some larger seeds must be soaked for 6 to 12 hours before planting). We added grow domes to our plant pods and selected the “vegetable” button on the top of the light panel, which put the grow light on the appropriate timer.

We love this system’s flexibility. It’s also on the smaller side, so it’s easy to find a spot for it, even in cramped spaces. Our biggest concern is that there isn’t much spacing between the pods, so depending on the plant, it can get crowded.

What our tester says: “The Ahopegarden was simple to set up. We love that it has automatic lights for growing fruits and flowers or vegetables. We planted dwarf tomatoes and mini bell peppers in our growing kit, and they sprouted within a week.”—Katie Barton, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Ahopegarden hydroponic system at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Setup 4/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 4/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 4/5

The AeroGarden Bounty grows up to nine plants and comes with a seed kit of the user’s choice. Thanks to a convenient touch screen, growers can easily set their own light and watering schedule, and there’s a vacation mode for when the system will be unattended.

One of the system’s best features is its tall grow height of 24 inches—the highest of any smaller hydroponic system in our lineup. The grow height makes it easier to nurture larger plant varieties, such as peppers and tomatoes, without worrying about plants getting their leaves singed on the lights. The system also includes a trellis, which is helpful when growing such larger plants.

The Bounty has a large water reservoir, so the system needs minimal topping off. It also comes with liquid plant food and humidity caps for seeds to germinate. However, in testing—growing a combination of lettuces and herbs—the width of the system proved a bit short. This led to stunted growth of some plants, while others competed for light. For example, when we placed cilantro and a short lettuce variety next to each other, the cilantro grew taller and blocked light from the lettuce, which failed to truly thrive.

While AeroGarden could fix this problem by making the Bounty wider, we found the solution to be simply using fewer grow stations simultaneously. When replanting seeds in the system during a second round of testing, we planted fewer plants (six instead of nine) and found that they did better, growing larger and looking healthier.

What our tester says: “Despite the width of the system being a bit short for my preferences, after I figured out how to work around this issue, the AeroGarden Bounty earned one of the best overall spots for the number of plants it grows, its reasonable price, its tall grow height, and for being an inclusive kit that makes hydroponics simple.”—Jenn Ryan, Product Reviews tester and writer

Few gardening processes are more straightforward than taking cuttings from existing houseplants or vines and starting them in water. While the system doesn’t include LED lights or a water-recirculating pump, it works via a tried-and-true plant-propagation method that is simple but effective. When roots develop, plants can be transplanted into pots or to an outdoor garden spot.

However, we found the necks of the glass vases to be quite narrow—while we could easily fit herbs (such as the rosemary we rooted), we had trouble getting snake plants and succulents into the water. The Lettuce Grow Farmstand has the capacity for 36 full-size plants, making it the largest hydroponic system on our list. It comes with a teardrop-shaped base that can hold 20 gallons of water, which means we didn’t have to top off the water reservoir as often as with some of the smaller systems.

The Click & Grow is an attractive indoor garden ideal for beginners or those with limited space. It comes with everything a user needs to get started, including plant pods, grow domes, and easy-to-follow instructions.

This small hydroponic system was a breeze to set up. All we had to do was insert the plant packs into the pods, add water, and plug the unit in. Even newbies can stretch their green thumb with this system from leading hydroponic systems manufacturer AeroGarden. The Harvest 2.0 indoor herb garden provides everything necessary to care for its six growing stations. We loved the simple setup: Gardeners simply insert plant pods, add water and plant food, plug in the unit, and it’s ready to grow. One downside to this indoor hydroponic garden is that it lacks an adjustable light timer—the lights simply come on for 15 hours a day, then turn off until the cycle starts again. Plantaform’s Smart Indoor Garden is a fogponics system that turns a fertilizer and water mixture into fog, delivering nutrients to the plant’s root system. It comes with 15 pods, a lettuce mix plant pack, germination domes, and plant food. Six other plant pack varieties are available for purchase separately.

When we received the Plantaform grow kit, we were impressed by its quality, futuristic look. While it’s a bit larger, at about two feet tall and almost two feet in diameter, we positioned it in the middle of our dining room table. The instructions for setting it up weren’t quite as clear as those for other growing systems we tried. However, once we figured out what to do, it only took about fifteen minutes to get everything set up.

Our lettuce seeds sprouted within a few days, and we were able to remove the germination domes. We then relied on the app to inform us when to add water and nutrients and harvest the plants. Unfortunately, the app malfunctioned a few times, telling us to harvest at one week and then again at two weeks when the plants were still tiny. We decided to ignore these notifications and wait until the plants were at least 40 to 45 days, as suggested on the Plantaform website. Despite issues with the app, keeping up with this hydroponic setup was as easy as refilling the water tank every two and a half weeks, and our lettuce plants grew to be lush and healthy.

Get the Plantaform hydroponics system at Plantaform.

When evaluating these hydroponic home garden systems, we considered over a dozen companies and looked at the brand, customer reviews, features of the product, extra items included, and how well the system grew plants. We also looked at durability and ease of use when testing and evaluating these products.

We scored each product using a rubric that evaluated the watering system, how well the plants in the system thrived, how easy the system was to set up and use, any extra features the product included, types of plants the system could grow, the durability of the product, and how attractive the setup was. We also considered the cost value of each product.

As we tested each hydroponic system, we looked closely at how well the plants grew and how easy the system was to use and maintain. To do this, we tested each system for a minimum of a month, and some of the systems were tested for over a year.

Plants need four essential elements to thrive: water, oxygen, light, and nutrients. A successful hydroponic system must supply an adequate amount of all four. For those new to cultivating an indoor garden, the options may seem confusing, but today’s manufacturers offer various types of hydroponic systems that automate much of the process.

While all hydroponic systems supply plant roots with water and nutrients, the method varies. There are six common types of hydroponic systems, all with unique strong points, but some are better suited to commercial settings than DIY home settings.

Hydroponic gardening at home is not difficult, but the operator will need basic knowledge about how hydroponics work. This means, for most systems, that growers should have some experience in sprouting plants from seeds, knowing when plants need plant food, monitoring the water flow of the reservoir, and adjusting nutrient levels and pH.

Fortunately, with today’s consumer hydroponic systems, indoor gardening is simple and straightforward. Systems like the popular AeroGarden come with mesh pods and soilless medium (often coconut coir plugs), as well as a pump for circulating water and keeping roots moist and healthy. Unlike classic terrariums, most of today’s in-home systems also feature grow lights on timers that provide the correct amount of light for optimal growth.

One of the convenient characteristics of a hydroponic grow system is that users can grow more plants in less space because the roots don’t need to spread out to seek nutrients. Depending on the type of setup, hydroponic systems can be as small as a few inches deep by a few inches wide or as big as a few feet deep by a few feet wide. The most common models, such as the AeroGarden Harvest, can fit on a kitchen countertop, ladder plant stand, or a table and take up no more than 1 to 2 square feet of space—yet some models can grow up to 30 full-size plants.

Indoor hydroponic systems can grow a wide variety of plant types. While smaller systems, such as the AeroGarden, are best used for herbs and smaller varieties of peppers and tomatoes, larger systems like the Lettuce Grow Farmstand can grow virtually anything, including large lettuces, full-size tomato or pepper plants, kale, Swiss chard, bok choy, and even cabbage. Flowers can be grown in hydroponic systems, too.

Consistent temperature is essential to plant growth, so commercial hydroponic growers often have water heaters to regulate the water temperature. However, in-home hydroponic systems don’t require the same temperature-control level because they’re usually placed in a home where the temperature remains between 60 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit. Many experts suggest that the optimal water temperature for plant growth is between 68 and 71.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

Unlike self-watering planter systems, a soilless growing medium is normally used in hydroponic gardening. These mediums can include coconut coir plugs or mineral wool. However, some systems, such as the Lettuce Grow Farmstand, have plants that are started in actual soil and then transplanted into small pods to grow without additional soil in the hydroponic system.

Some systems come with plants or seeds already in the substrate. As the plants grow, the roots extend below the pod into the reservoir or channel beneath.

Nutrients used in hydroponic systems can be in either powder or liquid form. Some come with powders that must be dissolved in warm water before being added to the water reservoir, while other systems come with liquid plant food that can be poured directly into the reservoir.

Automated hydroponic systems require minimal maintenance relative to a traditional garden or a DIY hydroponics system. Most systems recommend topping off the tank reservoir about once a week and adding plant food at the same time. It’s also recommended that the reservoir be cleaned every month or so to prevent the buildup of algae in the tank.

During the growing cycle, users may also need to wipe down the unit’s surface with a clean, damp rag to maintain its appearance—they aren’t immune to dust!

There are many advantages to owning a hydroponic grow kit, including water conservation, reduced risk of pest problems, and fresh produce year-round.

According to Dr. Michael B. Timmons, professor emeritus and graduate professor in the Department of Biological and Environmental Engineering at Cornell University, “Producing food as efficiently as possible and minimizing the use of our scarce resources should be a goal for everyone. Each family could contribute toward this goal by choosing to produce some or all of the vegetables they eat. Producing vegetables hydroponically using controlled environment agriculture (CEA) … uses 90 percent less water and land than conventional agriculture.” He goes on to say that those who grow some of their food hydroponically can reduce the associated carbon footprint by producing in their own home, garage, or mini-greenhouse.

As explained by the Oklahoma State University Extension, one of the advantages of utilizing a hydroponic system to grow vegetables and flowers is being able to control the nutrients and growing environment. Hydroponic systems also reduce the risk of chemical exposure due to pesticides as well as the risk of pests infesting the plants and soil (although the plants are not immune to pests that may travel indoors). Finally, with an all-inclusive hydroponic system, growing herbs, fruits, veggies, or flowers indoors needn’t take a lot of time or require a large garden or a sunny window.

Because hydroponic systems automate the growing process, users don’t need a lot of gardening or hydroponic knowledge to enjoy fresh herbs and produce. For those new to growing indoors, however, some questions are to be expected. Read on for answers that provide basic info.

For those just developing a green thumb, an affordable hydroponics system that automates lighting and watering and provides a few growing stations is ideal.

Most systems come with built-in aeration via a pump, so additional aeration is not needed.

No. Nutrient solutions are preformulated to offer the best pH level for a wide variety of plants and herbs. However, you may want to test the pH level of the water in the reservoir with a pH test kit and add pH-adjusting liquid to raise or lower the pH level to about 6 or 7, which is the ideal range for growing vegetables and herbs.

To maintain a strict pH level, pH-adjusting liquids are available, and a couple of drops of either “pH Up” or “pH Down” can change the level. Some hydroponic systems come with a testing kit, but these are often a separate purchase.

Yes. Each indoor growing system has its own recommendations on how often to clean it, and some systems recommend cleaning as often as once a month. In general, cleaning requires removing all the spent plants and scrubbing or wiping out the unit—especially the water reservoir—before using it again. Apart from that, wipe down the surfaces with a clean, damp rag as necessary to remove dust, plant debris, and grime.

Lunch boxes for construction workers need to keep food fresh, but they must also be highly portable and durable to meet the demands of their environments. To help you choose the right construction lunch box from the many options available, we researched the pros and cons of various lunch box materials and designs and reached out to two experts for their opinions. Based on our research and their insights, we chose the Arctic Zone Titan 16 Can Zipperless Hardbody Cooler as our top choice for its tough construction, easy-to-clean interior, and convenient shoulder strap. The Arctic Zone cooler has a thick base designed to keep ice for up to 2 days. Though the 16-can version has quite a large capacity, it’s actually quite comfortable to carry thanks to its padded, adjustable shoulder strap.

As a soft-sided cooler, the CleverMade doesn’t have the strength or durability of a hard-sided model, though the lined polyester fabric is lightweight and easy to wipe clean. The lunch box has handles and a strap for convenience, an incorporated bottle opener, and a large mesh pocket. Though the liner is leakproof, the insulated walls of the cooler aren’t super thick, so using blocks of ice might be smart since cubed ice won’t stay frozen long.

Get the CleverMade lunch box for construction workers at Amazon or CleverMade.

Well known for high-quality protective clothing for construction workers, Carhartt has designed its insulated lunch cooler to the same standards. The abrasion-resistant 600 denier polyester is triple stitched and protected by the brand’s Rain Defender water-repellent coating. Its zippers are the same heavyweight YKK versions used on other Carhartt products, including the best construction work pants.

The two main compartments inside this Carhartt deluxe lunch cooler provide versatile food storage and keep contents cool for 8 hours or more. You can access the top section separately from the bottom, and it also has a handy zippered pocket on the front. The bag’s handle and shoulder strap make it easy to carry, though we’re surprised the latter isn’t adjustable. Though obviously not as strong as a hard-sided model, the Carhartt cooler, one of our top lunch coolers for construction workers, is light, surprisingly rugged, and a great value.

Get the Tourit lunch box for construction workers at Amazon.

To choose the right lineup of lunch boxes for the varying needs of construction workers, we considered the amount of food and drink each option could carry as well as the holding temperatures they could maintain to keep consumable items safe and fresh. Durability and portability were also top priorities, as these lunch bags and boxes must be convenient to carry yet strong enough to hold up to rugged jobsites. Though we were also careful about selecting options to fit a range of budgets, we ruled out cheaply made, low-quality lunch boxes in favor of products that offer lasting value for long-term use.

Shawna Guevara, managing director at Landmark Structural Builders, confirms much of our own thinking. “A proper lunch box for construction workers should prioritize functionality and durability,” she says. “Workers don’t need zippers that break easily, lunch boxes that retain food odors, or ones that are difficult to clean.”

As you decide which lunch box is right for you, consider these expert insights from contractor Jay Sanders of remodeling specialists Maryland Contractors regarding which features to look for when shopping for women’s and men’s lunch boxes for work. For Jay, “a tight-fitting lid that keeps food at the desired temperature for hours” and “chemical-free lunch boxes for meals that don’t harm your health” are the most important considerations.

Since lunch boxes designed for the office or coolers for the beach may not stand up to the rigors of the jobsite, evaluating construction worker lunch boxes based on the following key elements will ensure you get the right product for your needs.

Lunch boxes aren’t always treated with the greatest care. Those that have a tough outer shell will be more resistant to damage from the knocks and bumps that are part of life on a busy construction site. Hard-sided lunch boxes can help prevent food from getting smashed, and some are even strong enough to sit on while you eat. Though they are more durable, their construction can make them a bit heavier, bulkier, and less portable.

On the other hand, soft-sided and collapsible coolers are quite portable. They’re almost always lighter than hard models, are a snap to store, and are frequently less expensive. Though soft-sided coolers don’t provide as much protection for their contents as hard options, a soft lunch box can be a perfectly viable option if your lunch will wait in a vehicle rather than be toted directly to the site.

Capacity requirements largely depend on how big a meal you typically pack. A larger capacity may be more versatile—it can be used for a family weekend outing, for example. Conversely, the best small coolers will be sized just right for single-meal use as well as more portable and easier to store.

Capacity descriptions vary. Often, they are given as a number of standard beverage cans, making capacity fairly easy to visualize. Quart capacity is another common measurement. Those given in inches can make it difficult to picture the true size, so it may be smart to fold some cardboard into roughly the measurements given to avoid ordering a lunch box that’s too small or large.

Multiple compartments (as often found in bento boxes) are convenient for those who take various items for lunch and wish to keep them separated. One of our top picks even includes a pill organizer.

A well-insulated construction lunch box can keep food cool or warm for some time. However, while some manufacturers indicate how long they expect the contents to maintain temperature, their estimates may be optimistic, and there isn’t any recognized standard for the amount of insulation a lunch box or cooler provides. Shoppers should use their best judgment: Look at the thickness of the insulation, how rugged the fabric and seams are, and how well the insulated area closes.

How a construction worker lunch box is carried and how easily it opens and closes is also worth considering, so examine the soundness of handles and clasps. Those likely to pack ice in the lunch box should also check how leakproof it is, particularly with soft cool boxes.

All aspects of jobsite safety are important—even regarding your lunch box. Certain products previously used to produce plastics are now deemed unsafe for use with food. The organic compound bisphenol A (known as BPA) is one of the main culprits, though PVC and phthalates (which make plastics more flexible) should also be avoided. Many manufacturers will state whether their plastic containers are free of these materials. Since food hygiene is a crucial part of food safety, remember also to consider how easy it will be to thoroughly wash all areas of the container.

The guide above contains useful information and vetted products to help you choose the best lunch box for construction workers. Anyone with additional questions about how to choose and use a rugged, reliable lunch box will find more information below.

As with the best coolers, keeping lunch cold in a lunch box is best accomplished by using an insulated ice bag or box with ice blocks or bags of ice inside.

Hot soups and stews will maintain the desired temperature inside an insulated container or vacuum bottle. Plug-in warmers like the Travelisimo Electric Heated Lunch Box can also heat meals so long as a wall outlet or DC port is available.

The body can absorb aluminum through contact with food. However, many sources say it passes through naturally and does not present health problems. Some aluminum lunch boxes are specifically marked as food safe.

The best way to clean most lunch boxes is with a sponge and warm, soapy water, though the manufacturer may have its own suggestions, and these should take priority.

Health experts often suggest you replace your lunch box every year since even the best options can accumulate small amounts of mold and bacteria in hard-to-clean crevices. If damaged, a lunch box should be replaced immediately to prevent any risk of contamination.

Generally speaking, no, lunch boxes are not microwavable. If you need a microwavable container, consider packing something like these PrepNaturals glass meal-prep containers inside your lunch box.

Stainless steel lunch boxes aren’t necessarily better than plastic ones. However, they are a lightweight and durable option, especially for construction workers. This Stanley Classic 10-Quart Lunch Box is one of our absolute favorite steel lunch boxes.

#7767. School Board Can Order High School Teacher to Remove "Hate Has No Home Here" Rainbow Poster

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From McIntyre v. Little Miami School Dist., decided Monday by Judge Matthew McFarland (S.D. Ohio) (appeal pending):

Plaintiff George McIntyre is a teacher at Little Miami High School, a school within Defendant Little Miami School District ("District"), where he teaches American History and Advanced Placement European History. McIntyre placed a poster in his classroom displaying the slogan "Hate Has No Home Here" ("Poster"), depicted below:

As shown above, the Poster features five hands holding hearts filled with distinct symbols, including the American flag, a peace sign, the rainbow pride flag, and the transgender pride flag. McIntyre hung up the Poster to remind his students to "treat all their classmates with mutual respect, regardless of personal opinions or beliefs." …

The District's "longstanding practice" has been to permit teachers to decorate their classrooms and display personal items. That latitude, however, is "defined by" the District's Little Miami School Board ("Board") policy.

That policy landscape shifted when the Ohio General Assembly enacted House Bill 8, known as the Ohio Parents' Bill of Rights. That statute requires school districts to provide parental notice and review for materials containing "sexuality content" and allows parents to opt out for alternative assignments. "[S]exuality content" is defined as "oral or written instruction, presentation, image, or description of sexual concepts or gender ideology in a classroom setting," but explicitly excludes "[i]ncidental references to sexual concepts or gender ideology occurring outside of formal instruction or presentations on such topics." On October 28, 2025, the Board adopted Board Policy 5780.01, incorporating the statute's definitions and notice/opt-out requirements into District policy.

The Board considered restricting classroom wall-hangings exclusively to the U.S. flag, the Ohio flag, and school-related displays, but ultimately concluded that state law and Board Policy 5780.01 provided sufficient oversight. Under District guidance, concerns that a classroom display contains "sexuality content" under state law or Board Policy 5780.01 are subject to a three-tiered review: first by the school principal, then on appeal to the superintendent, and finally to the Board….

In September 2025, Defendant David Wallace, the Board President, visited McIntyre's classroom and photographed the Poster. Thereafter, Wallace contacted District Superintendent Regina Morgan, requesting that McIntyre remove the Poster. Morgan relayed the request to Little Miami High School's Principal, Kevin Harleman.

Harleman spoke with McIntyre about the Poster, and asked whether McIntyre tied the display to his curriculum or classroom discussions, or if it was simply a decorative wall hanging. On February 2, 2026, McIntyre emailed Harleman, identifying specific content standards within the model curriculum for his classes that he felt the Poster was "especially applicable" to. McIntyre further noted that, while the Poster applied to those broad historical themes, it was not used as a formal instructional device and instead was "a reminder that [his students] must treat their classmates with mutual respect." Harleman forwarded that email to Morgan.

The next day, Morgan informed Wallace that, upon her review, while the Poster contained sexual identity symbols, she did not "believe a reasonable observer would conclude its primary purpose [was] to prompt discussion, provide instruction, or solicit student engagement on sexual concepts or gender ideology." Under the "display guidelines," Morgan acknowledged that it was "now a Board decision as to how to move forward." …

[On February 25, t]he Board voted 4 to 1 to classify the Poster as sexuality content under Board Policy 5780.01 and ordered its immediate removal from McIntyre's classroom….

The court rejected McIntyre's claim that the Board's actions violated his First Amendment rights:

Although public employees "undoubtably enjoy certain rights," those rights "do not transform them into 'sovereigns unto themselves.'" Rather, "the government, just like a private employer, retains 'control over what the employer itself has commissioned or created': the employee's job." That authority carries particular significance in the context of public education, where Ohio's compulsory-attendance requirements give public school teachers "a captive audience for their in-class speech." …

[Thus], the Sixth Circuit has held that a public school teacher's in-class curricular and pedagogical choices are not protected by the First Amendment. In reaching this holding, the Sixth Circuit reasoned that "[w]hen a teacher teaches, the school system does not regulate that speech as much as it hires that speech. Expression is a teacher's stock in trade, the commodity [ ]he sells to [his] employer in exchange for a salary." Since Ohio law left curriculum choices to elected school boards as "an accountability measure," those boards are entitled to "regulate the content of what is or is not expressed" on their behalf….

Here, McIntyre spoke as a public employee pursuant to his official duties when displaying the Poster in his classroom. McIntyre hung the Poster to foster a respectful environment among his students and later identified specific state curriculum standards that he believed the Poster supported…. McIntyre's motivations and actions were directly related to, and arose from his professional responsibilities as a teacher shaping his students' learning environment.

Whether McIntyre used the Poster for formal instruction is immaterial. He gained access to and control over the classroom wall space through his position as a public school employee, not as a private citizen. His ability to maintain classroom displays thus existed within the scope of that public employment, which the Board regulated through established policies. As McIntyre displayed the Poster pursuant to his official duties, his expression constituted unprotected employee speech.

Contrary to McIntyre's argument, the Supreme Court's holding in Kennedy v. Bremerton School Dist. (2022) does not alter this conclusion. Unlike the high school coach in Kennedy, who offered a brief prayer while essentially "off the clock" after a game, McIntyre maintained a permanent display on his classroom wall that was visible during school hours. Managing the classroom environment during the school day relates to his job responsibilities, not private citizen speech. Kennedy thus does not compel a finding that McIntyre spoke as a private citizen…. The Board was [thus] entitled to restrain [McIntyre's] speech, and McIntyre is not entitled to declaratory judgment that his First Amendment rights were violated….

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7765. 3 Winterization Projects That Are as Easy as Painting

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 11, 2026 10:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Winter weather can be devastating to outdoor furniture, appliances, and structures, which is why many people store as much as possible in a covered shed or garage throughout the cold season. Even though not everything can be neatly tucked away, such as your deck, walkways, and gates, you can take steps to prepare them for harsh winter conditions before snow starts to fall.

Outdoor winterization projects that involve painting, staining, or sealing help surfaces create a durable barrier against freeze-thaw cycles, moisture intrusion, and corrosive deicing salts. It’s important to complete these protective jobs before the first hard freeze so you can prevent deep structural damage during the winter months.

Leaving wood decks, fences, or patio furniture bare during winter allows moisture from snow and ice to seep into the wood pores. When trapped water freezes, it expands, causing the wood to split, warp, and rot. A fresh coat of waterproof sealant or oil-based stain acts as a hydrophobic barrier. Water pools on top of the sealed surface rather than penetrating the wood grain.

Before applying a compatible exterior stain or water-repellent finish, clean the surface, remove failing finish, and allow the wood to dry sufficiently. For decking and steps, choose a winterization product specifically approved for horizontal surfaces and foot traffic.

Marc Sharkey, owner of Dynamic Painting Inc, says that “the finish reduces water absorption from rain and melting snow. Repeated wetting and drying can contribute to checking, splitting, and warping; prolonged dampness also creates conditions for decay.

“Pay particular attention to exposed board ends and areas where the old finish has worn away.” He also warns: “A new coating cannot repair rotten wood.” Given that Sharkey’s business is based in Alberta, he has experience dealing with some of the harshest winters in North America.

This oil-based formula provides corrosion resistance and weather protection for outdoor metal surfaces . Learn more in our buyer’s guide.

Winter preparation is important to safeguard your home. Chipped paint on steel or iron railings, furniture, and gates exposes the raw metal to oxygen and winter humidity, rapidly accelerating the oxidation process. Road salt or salt-based sidewalk ice melts further expedite this corrosion, eating through the metal structures. Applying a coat of exterior, rust-resistant enamel or oil-based paint seals out moisture and oxygen, halting the chemical reaction that creates rust.

It’s a budget-friendly winterization project that also forms a slick, chemical-resistant barrier against salt splash-back. Before applying a coating, remove loose rust and flaking paint and clean away dirt and salt. Then apply an appropriate rust-inhibiting primer and exterior metal finish. Check compatibility carefully: steel, aluminum, and galvanized metal can require different preparation and primers.

“An intact coating limits exposure to moisture and oxygen, helping slow corrosion. Left exposed, rust can spread beneath surrounding paint, causing more peeling and pitting. Over time, severe corrosion can weaken components. Painting over loose rust does not solve the underlying problem,” explains Sharkey.

Moisture from ice and snow can cause significant damage to concrete because it is a highly porous material. When snow melts on walkways, driveways, or patios, the concrete absorbs the water. Subsequent freezing temperatures cause that internal water to expand, which leads to surface flaking, scaling, and deep cracking.

Unlike surface coatings, penetrating sealers chemically bond inside concrete pores. They create an invisible, breathable hydrophobic barrier that prevents liquid water from sinking into the stone, while still allowing internal vapor to escape.

Sharkey notes that “for compatible, absorbent concrete steps, walkways, or patios, a penetrating sealer rated for exterior concrete and freeze-thaw exposure can reduce water absorption. Confirm compatibility with any existing treatment and follow the preparation instructions.”

Reducing water and deicing-salt penetration helps protect against winter deterioration. However, just keep in mind that a sealer is preventive maintenance; it does not repair cracks, failing concrete, or drainage problems.

#7764. National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.  The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.  While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

#7763. 2 BigLaw firms face proposed class actions over cyber breaches

In newly filed proposed class action lawsuits, plaintiffs are alleging that cyberattacks at Baker McKenzie and Squire Patton Boggs led to exposure of their personal information. (Image from Shutterstock)

In newly filed proposed class action lawsuits, plaintiffs are alleging that cyberattacks at Baker McKenzie and Squire Patton Boggs led to exposure of their personal information.

The complaint against Baker McKenzie was filed in the Northern District of Illinois on Wednesday. According to Reuters, Baker McKenzie said last week a cybercriminal in August “socially engineered two of our users” to obtain a limited number of files, but that “there was no independent malicious access to our system.”

Squire Patton Boggs disclosed its breach in October, saying it involved “an unauthorized third party obtaining a limited set of information from the firm,” Reuters reports.

The complaint against Squire Patton Boggs was also filed Wednesday but in the Northern District of Ohio.

Neither law firm responded to requests for comment from Reuters.

Nonstick sprays for snow blowers lubricate chutes and augers to help prevent clogging and buildup, making these helpful machines easier to use. However, since many snow blower sprays appear relatively similar at first glance, it can be hard to know which one to choose. To aid you in your decision, we reached out to an expert for their opinion and tested eight popular options. In addition to using the sprays on our snow blower, we also applied them to several electric snow shovels to better understand their unique properties.

Based on our research, expert insights, and testing across various tools and materials, we chose the DuPont Snow & Ice Repellent Nonstick Clear Coating as our top pick. It dries quickly, is long-lasting, and prevents clogging from both powdery and wet snow, which could otherwise lead to frustrating interruptions. Read on to see how this product and the rest of our top picks performed and why they earned a spot on our list of the best nonstick sprays for snow blowers.

Bottom line: DuPont's Snow & Ice Repellent stands out as the best nonstick spray for snow blowers, offering quick-drying and long-lasting protection. Explore other top picks for specific needs and budgets.

We selected each of the following best nonstick sprays for snow blowers based on performance, ease of use, and overall value.

The DuPont Teflon snow and ice repellent spray is specifically made to create nonstick surfaces that repel moisture in liquid or frozen form. The Teflon fluoropolymer and silicone combination adheres well to metal, rubber, or plastic, creating a barrier between those materials and snow and ice that would otherwise cause chute clogging and auger buildup.

As with any nonstick spray, the product adheres best when the surface it’s applied to is dry. After wiping down our snow blower’s chute and auger, we sprayed on a consistent coating of the Teflon snow and ice and left everything to dry. We periodically pressed a finger against the sprayed surface to test for readiness, and after about 10 minutes, the coating was completely set. During the long snow-clearing session that followed, the chute didn’t clog once and the coating had plenty of coverage remaining to handle the next storm.

Read our full review: DuPont Snow & Ice Repellent Nonstick Clear Coating

What our tester says: “When testing this spray with our snow blower, we were careful to hit a combination of powder and a few slushy patches that would usually be difficult for the chute to clear. The powder flew through the snow blower chute without issue, and the wet snow did as well.”—Zach Lazzari, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the DuPont snow & ice nonstick spray for snow blowers at Amazon or Ace Hardware.

Liquid Wrench silicone spray for snow blowers is an aerosol spray with a heavy silicone base that sticks well to slick surfaces to provide optimum nonstick performance. Since silicone is a natural water repellent, it works for everything from creating a waterproof barrier to fixing squeaky hinges and inhibiting rust.

For snow blowing specifically, this Liquid Wrench spray proved to be an excellent lubricant: While running through a walkway and driveway covered in wet snow, the chute remained clean and didn’t clog once. Get the DuPont Dry Film nonstick spray for snow blowers at Amazon or Ace Hardware.

When we hit a section of gravel and dirt we’ve known to be hard on augers and chutes, the CRC formula maintained a nice slick surface and didn’t seem phased by the abrasive snow. As for the fishing rod? It smoothed out its gear performance with plenty of lubrication. Turns out the ample dose of silicone in CRC absolutely does deliver a heavy-duty performance.

PrB’laster advanced dry lube spray is designed to lubricate saws, machine parts, and moving elements of machinery without leaving any sticky residue behind. Unlike many of the products we tested, it does not use silicone and also does not contain chlorinated solvents. This means it evaporates quickly and won’t interfere with mechanical functions.

As a dry lubricant, we noted it set immediately after application, creating a layer of protection that didn’t attract or trap dirt and debris. During testing, our favorite thing about this product was its unique spray-top design. Its aerosol system has a nozzle that rotates into position, making it easy to hit crevices and hard-to-reach places. The push button also has a big thumbprint that makes it incredibly easy to control. When not in use, the nozzle folds down and out of place.

Adding to its ease of use, this formula stays effective at a wide range of temperatures between -100 to 500 degrees Fahrenheit. If you have a machine needing attention in tight cracks and difficult places, you’ll want to give the WD-40 silicone spray for your snow blower​ a try.

What our expert says: We asked Gene Caballero, co-founder of GreenPal, an app that connects those needing snow removal and lawn care with a local provider, which nonstick snow blower spray he prefers. He said, “WD-40 Specialist Silicone and Fluid Film have always worked well for me. They not only prevent clogs but also protect your snow blower from corrosion caused by wet, salty conditions.”

Get the WD-40 nonstick spray for snow blowers at Lowe’s, The Home Depot, or Walmart.

After researching and comparing product features and reviews for dozens of nonstick snow blower sprays, we narrowed our testing list to eight products. As our property in Montana got hit with one winter storm after another, we had plenty of snow to work through as well as very cold weather, so we got to work lubricating several gas snow blowers, cordless snow blowers, and electric snow blowers with each of our chosen products.

We applied each snow blower nonstick spray in a dry location, fully covering the chutes, augers, interior boxes, and passageways. A large portion of our work coincided with our tests on snow blowers for gravel driveways, meaning the sprays were all used in particularly rough conditions since the snow contained dirt and hard particles. We also tested them on shovels, plow blades, door locks, and other surfaces needing lubrication to get a comprehensive idea of how long each spray remained effective, their ease of application, and their overall performance.

Before choosing a nonstick spray, take a few minutes to learn what to look for, including drying time, safety concerns, functions, and the spray’s longevity.

The drying time for a spray wax for snow blowers will vary depending on the specific product, the temperature and humidity of the environment, and the moisture content in the snow blower’s chute. Products that dry quickly are generally easier to use since they make applying a second layer when needed faster so you can get to work sooner.

Applying the nonstick snow and ice repellent in a warm, dry environment, like a garage or workshop, is ideal. Warmth helps the spray stick to the metal and dry quickly. Users can apply sprays to damp surfaces in freezing temperatures, but it will take longer for the spray to dry. Until the spray is completely dry, it won’t lubricate properly, nor will it be fully water- or corrosion-resistant.

While nonstick sprays for snow blowers are helpful in preventing clogs, they often contain chemicals that warrant handling them with care. We recommend you check the product’s label for safe application recommendations and to see if it contains any hazardous materials.

Generally speaking, you’ll want to keep snow blower sprays out of reach of children and pets since they can be toxic if ingested or inhaled. It’s a good idea to use these products in a well-ventilated space and consider wearing eye protection, a respirator, and gloves. Because the liquid spray may be flammable until it dries, store it away from sources of heat or flames.

The primary purpose of a nonstick spray for snow blowers is to lubricate the inside of the snow blower chute to keep snow from sticking and clogging the chute. However, many nonstick sprays have additional benefits, such as preventing rust, protecting against ultraviolet (UV) damage, resisting water, or even adding a shine to metal finishes.

Longevity refers to the length of time a nonstick spray remains effective after application. Every nonstick spray we tested must be reapplied frequently, though some worked well through several uses. Generally speaking, they all need to be reapplied every few uses at a minimum.

When working through a really difficult storm, consider reapplying nonstick spray after every use to keep the machine performing optimally. Always apply a fresh coat ahead of storms and continue renewing the coating as needed throughout the season. Even if you go through a couple of cans in the winter, you will still save money removing snow yourself rather than paying the cost of professional snow removal.

Learn more about nonstick spray for snow blowers by reading the answers to these frequently asked questions.

Snow blower chutes can clog because you’re trying to push through the snow too fast. They also clog when the heavy snow has a high moisture content and forms compact clumps that stick to the sides of the chute.

You can use normal WD-40 to help lubricate the auger and moving parts on a snow blower. Use the silicone version of the product to add a nonstick layer of protection on the snow blower chute and auger. It’s easy to apply, dries quickly, and acts as a water repellent and corrosion inhibitor.

Snow blower spray is easy to use: Just shake the can, remove the lid, and spray an even coating inside the chute and to the auger. The nonstick spray lubricant makes the chute and auger slippery, preventing snow from sticking and clogging the blower.

For a complete set of instructions regarding snow blower maintenance, see our guide on how to maintain a snow blower. While the specific maintenance steps your machine requires will depend on the type of snow blower you have, general steps include checking all fittings and components, changing oil or charging batteries, and lubricating the drive and chassis.

#7760. The President Nominates Circuit Judges, Not Senators

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Circuit seats belong to the circuit, and not to the state.

There has been a momentous shift in the relationship between the President and the Senate, and most people have missed it.

Let's start with the Eighth Circuit. The Trump Administration interviewed Justice Cody Hiland, but determined he was not up to the task of being a circuit judge, so they offered him a federal district court seat as a consolation prize. Hiland shot back at the White House Counsel and refused the seat. He even wanted to rub it in Trump's face. The White House made a stellar nomination with Judge Lee Rudofsky. Hiland then told an entire room of law students about his experience as a lesson that should be learned. But Hiland had a friend in a high place. Senator Boozman of Arkansas lobbied Senator Tillis of North Carolina and Senator Cornyn of Texas to block Judge Rudofsky.

Apparently there were some discussions between the President and Boozman, and the President folded. Maybe Trump determined that he needed as many judges confirmed before January, so the identity of the judge didn't matter. Maybe Trump didn't want to create more problems with his caucus. Maybe Trump just didn't care. Who knows? Trump withdrew Rudofsky and nominated Hiland. There is no guarantee that Hiland gets a hearing and makes it through the process. We are so late in the game. And frankly, I wouldn't blame some of the other conservative senators from the Eighth Circuit for putting Hiland through the paces at the hearing. It's not clear to me he'll be able to answer all the questions. But regardless of what happens, Senator Boozman won and President Trump lost.

Now, onto my home, the Fifth Circuit. It is painfully clear there was some sort of deal between Judge Southwick and Senator Wicker. In no universe would the White House have picked Todd Butler without that deal. I've yet to hear anyone provide me a single shred of evidence that he is conservative beyond saying "All southern lawyers are conservative. Plus he's a Christian." What about Nathan Johnson and James Talarico? Moreover, Southwick announced on September 29 that he would take Senior Status, making it virtually impossible for another nominee to be selected.

Yesterday, I watched Butler's confirmation hearing with interest. He received a few softballs from Senator Grassley, a very warm welcome from Senator Kennedy, and some surprisingly nice questions from Senator Booker about representing police officers. Butler did not seem to understand departmentalism and mis-cited Marbury v. Madison. His answers were not particularly articulate--roughly on par with his oral argument before the Supreme Court. There was no depth or curiosity conveyed.  I actually think Butler tripped up on Senator Blumenthal's questions about January 6 and the election, but it didn't matter. He sailed through. Members of the conservative legal movement have raised doubts about Butler. But there were no tough questions asked by Senators Cruz, Lee, Hawley, Schmidt, or others. Only they know why they stayed out. Senator Wicker prevailed, and the President lost.

Then there is the bizarre situation in Oklahoma. Someone yesterday asked me if I knew what Senator Armstrong was doing. My response was, "Who is Senator Armstrong?" He is the temporary senator appointed to fill Senator Mullins's seat. As Mike Fragoso relays, Armstrong is blocking the nomination of Zach West to the District Court in Oklahoma. This is all about some sort of squabble between West and defeated-AG Drummond. Armstrong returned a blue slip but is now trying to take it back. That's not how things work. If Armstrong prevails here, the President will lose.

Circuit seats belong to the circuit, and not to the state. It bothers me that "home state" senators introduce circuit court nominees. That pageantry reinforces the wrong message. Hiland's seat does not belong to Arkansas and Butler's seat does not belong to Mississippi.

Unfortunately, Trump's surrender here has created a terrible precedent. Should the Republicans ever again return to power, I would hope this entire process is reconsidered. Circuit court nominees should be treated as "at large" seats. Senators can make recommendations, but they cannot dictate who is picked. Worse, judges (like Southwick) should not be allowed to make these deals. We should not tolerate incentive structure where motivated actors can control who represents an entire circuit. Maybe the better approach is to start consulting with all the Senators in a given circuit on possible picks, and then pick the best athlete.

Today, a federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Halima Salman, 27, a U.S. citizen and former resident of Brooklyn, also known as “Umm Khattab al-Muhajir,” of receiving military-type training from the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS), a designated foreign terrorist organization, in Syria. Salman was convicted after a two-week trial before U.S. District Judge Natasha C. Merle.

“The atrocities committed by ISIS, including mass executions, sexual slavery, and the systematic terrorizing of civilian populations, represent some of the gravest crimes of our time,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “There is simply no excuse for aligning with or receiving military training from an organization responsible for such suffering. Today's verdict sends a clear message that those who support this death cult will be found and prosecuted.”

“With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our Office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign.”

“It’s been nearly a decade since Halima Salman sought military training from ISIS in Syria, and today justice has been served,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI remains unwavering in its vigilance. We will continue to identify, disrupt, and bring to justice those who support foreign terrorist organizations and threaten the safety of our nation and our communities.”

As proven at trial, in September and October 2016, Salman’s parents traveled with her and her eight siblings out of the United States, ultimately destined for ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.

In late 2016 or early 2017, Salman was 18 years old and married to an ISIS fighter in Syria, where she voluntarily sought military-type training and received authorization to carry ammunition and an assault rifle from ISIS. Salman received a document certifying that she successfully completed that training, a copy of which was found on her husband’s cellphone after it was recovered from the battlefield. Also on her husband’s device were photos depicting Salman with an ISIS flag in the background and a video that shows her brandishing an AK-47 rifle.

The case was investigated by the FBI New York Field Office. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance obtaining evidence overseas.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Adam Amir and Amanda Shami for the Eastern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Reich, Paralegal Specialist Emily Woodruff and Trial Attorney Patrick Cashman of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

To provide shoppers with a list of top picks for snow thrower and snow blower oils, we primarily considered oil type and viscosity.

Oil type: Synthetic oil is the best choice for snow blower motors because it can handle lower temperatures and resist breakdown better than conventional oil.

Viscosity: Our recommendations are all variations of 5W-30, which is the ideal oil viscosity for snow blowers. The products we selected include budget-friendly versions for occasional use and heavier-duty options that come at a slightly higher price point. Most of the picks on our list are also versatile enough for other home and garden equipment and suitable for both cold and hot weather conditions.

The right oil can make the difference between a snow blower not starting because it has a gummed-up engine and one that kicks on without issue. Ahead, learn how viscosity, snow blower oil type, and other factors affect engine performance in a snow blower.

Gas-powered snow blowers use 4-cycle engine oil, a type of oil for snow blower engines that uses separate tanks for gas and oil, much like car engines. The gas fuels the engine, while the oil lubricates it.

Smaller engines, such as those on chainsaws, have 2-cycle engines. This type of small engine uses an oil and gas mixture that goes into one tank. Don’t use 2-cycle engine oil in a snow blower, as it will not properly lubricate the engine and will damage it. The motors on electric snow blowers don’t require engine oil.

Identifying the right type of engine oil is easy. The oil container has “4-cycle” or “2-cycle” clearly printed on the label. Although some 4-cycle engine oils are labeled for “small engines,” they are actually the same oil commonly used in cars and trucks.

Viscosity refers to the thickness of the oil. Higher viscosity oil is better at protecting and lubricating engines at high temperatures and peak load (high RPMs). Oil with a low viscosity remains thinner at lower temperatures, promoting better flow through the engine, making it easier to start and more efficient to run.

Viscosity is based on a scale created by SAE International, formerly known as the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE). Motor oil has two viscosity ratings:

Since snow blowers operate exclusively in cold weather, they typically use SAE 5W-30 weight oil, which ensures the engine will start at low temperatures. Make sure to check the maintenance section of your operating manual for the proper snow blower oil weight for your machine.

Not all 5W-30 engine oils are the same. Some engine oils are synthetic, which means they use higher-quality base oils than conventional oils. Synthetic lubricants can generally withstand higher temperatures and resist breakdown better. This means synthetic oil in a snow blower will last at least 50 percent longer than conventional oil, so you’ll probably need to perform less frequent snow blower maintenance.

Many synthetic oils also contain additives to help improve engine performance and extend engine life. Additives include detergents that flush grime and buildup and chemicals that coat engine parts to enhance lubrication.

For these reasons, synthetic oils are generally more expensive, often costing several times more than conventional oils. Still, proper maintenance of a quality snow blower will likely run you less than the cost of snow removal if you live in an area with relatively frequent snowfalls.

The 4-cycle engine oil that snow blowers use is the same oil used in any 4-cycle engine, which means it’s also an appropriate oil for lawn mowers, power washers, and even cars and trucks. 5W-30 oil provides adequate protection during both cold and warm weather.

Engine oil generally comes in 1-quart bottles, which is ideal for snow blowers since they hold about that much. It also comes in 5-quart containers and large, multi-gallon drums, but since its shelf life is generally around 5 years, it’s important not to buy more than you need. To store 5W-30 oil, keep it tightly sealed in a cool, dry environment.

Yes, synthetic options are likely the best oils for snow blowers. Synthetic oils are refined to run cleaner, leaving fewer deposits in the engine. Many also include additives that clean grime and sludge from the engine to improve performance.

Snow blowers operate in frigid temperatures, so the most important factor to consider is viscosity. Use motor oil with a low-temperature viscosity rating, such as 5W-30, to ensure the snow blower starts easily and runs smoothly.

Adding too much oil to a snow blower, or any 4-cycle engine, will cause the oil to rise and come in contact with other moving parts around the engine, aerating the oil and creating a huge mess.

According to Chris Urato, owner-operator of Urato Landscaping, LLC, you should perform a snow blower oil change “after the first 5 hours of use for new snow blowers, then every 20 to 50 hours of operation or once per season, depending on usage.”

A well-maintained snow blower should last around 10 to 15 years, but actual lifespan will depend on build quality and frequency of use. Performing regular maintenance tasks and avoiding common snow blower mistakes will help your machine last as long as possible.

“Yes, running it dry prevents stale fuel from gumming up the carburetor and causing maintenance issues,” says Chris Urato, a landscaper and snow-removal provider from Goshen, New York.

If you have a gas snow blower, you can give it 2 to 5 minutes before use so oil has time to run through the engine and lubricate it. If you have a battery-powered blower, there’s no need to let it warm up.

Following a few energy-saving strategies when setting the temperature on your thermostat can make a big difference in winter. According to the U.S. Department of Energy, it’s possible to save 10 percent a year on energy bills by being conservative with thermostat settings year-round.

We consulted an HVAC expert about thermostat-setting strategies during the coldest months of the year, and how we can save on energy costs. Here’s what he said.

“I prefer setting the thermostat to around 68 degrees Fahrenheit (20 degrees Celsius) during the day. This temperature strikes a balance between comfort and energy efficiency,” says Josh Mitchell, HVAC technician and founder of Air Conditioner Lab. “At night, lowering it to about 65 degrees Fahrenheit (18 degrees Celsius) is comfortable for sleeping and helps save on heating costs.”

According to the Department of Energy, setting your thermostat to the lowest comfortable temperature, which is typically 68 degrees Fahrenheit in the winter, helps slow down heat loss for homes with a regular furnace or baseboard heating system. However, that’s not the case for homes with heat pumps. Dialing down the thermostat too much can make a heat pump less efficient.

Everyone has a different comfort zone when it comes to temperatures. Just because 68 degrees can be an ideal temperature for a house in terms of reducing energy consumption doesn’t mean it’s right for everyone. Some people may prefer to set the thermostat slightly higher, at 70 degrees, and that’s okay.

The  Amazon Smart Thermostat uses Alexa to adjust the thermostat based on whether it thinks you’re home. Read the review.

It’s important to install a thermostat in the right location to prevent inaccurate temperature readings. Called ‘ghost readings,’ a thermostat may be triggered to run unnecessarily if placed near drafts, sunlight, and doorways. If air flow near the thermostat is blocked by furniture, also may not run effectively.

Mitchell says that the best place to locate a thermostat is on an interior wall that experiences the natural air flow in the home and is away from direct sunlight, drafts, doorways, and windows.

Your body requires time to adapt to slightly cooler temperatures. So there’s no need to (literally) go cold turkey when cooler outdoor temps arrive. Lower the temperature gradually, so you have time to adjust to being a little chilly. Until you acclimate, wear layers, don warm socks, and have a snuggly blanket on hand.

Regardless of how low you set the thermostat, you won’t save on your heating bill if your furnace or heating system works inefficiently. Make sure to do the following:

“Setting the thermostat too high in winter can lead to excessive energy consumption and higher utility bills,” Mitchell explains. “Conversely, setting it too low might not provide adequate comfort and could even risk pipes freezing. The key is to find a balanced setting that ensures comfort without overburdening your heating system.”

RELATED: Can Your Utility Company Control Your Home’s Thermostat?

Consider investing in a programmable thermostat that’ll automatically adjust the temperature for you. Programmable thermostats are ideal for people with consistent schedules.

“I’m a strong advocate for smart thermostats,” Mitchell says. “They offer advanced features like learning your schedule, remote control via a smartphone app, and energy usage reports, which not only enhances energy efficiency but also contributes to a more comfortable living environment.”

If your day-to-day routine is a bit more haphazard than a regular 9 to 5, consider a smart thermostat. Helpful features of some smart thermostats include settings that automatically detect your absence and lower the thermostat temperature while you’re gone. Some units can adjust the indoor temperature based on weather data.

“The ability to monitor and adjust your home’s temperature settings from anywhere can lead to cost savings and reduce your carbon footprint,” Mitchell explains.

Unless you work from home, turning the thermostat down during the workday can mean big savings on your energy bill. If you have pets, of course, you’ll want to set the thermostat to a temperature that will keep them comfortable while you’re gone. Still, the exact comfort zone will vary depending on the kind of pet and the animal’s size.

Another good opportunity to lower your thermostat is while you sleep. After all, research suggests that most people sleep poorly in overly warm conditions.

#7756. Man Pleads Guilty to Federal Hate Crimes in Deadly Attack on Boulder, Colorado, Gathering

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”

“By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution.  We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.
