#7685. The Giggler: The forgotten serial killer who haunted Boston’s South Station

Boston’s South Station was less than 70 years old in 1969 but seemed much older. It certainly lacked the glamour of nearby North Station, home to the Boston Garden, where the city’s basketball and hockey teams played and where the Rolling Stones and James Brown performed for screaming teenagers. In comparison, the South Station stop on 700 Atlantic Avenue was a dreary place for tired daily commuters on their way to the suburbs of the South Shore. With its high-domed ceiling and rickety escalators built during the Depression era, South Station managed to be both enormous and decrepit, a sickly old giant in need of urgent care. As the Boston Globe said a few years later, the once thriving railroad stop was “now staggering along in the last stages of neglect.”

Yet even as it faced the threat of the wrecking ball, the station remained busy, particularly at holiday time. On Friday, December 26, a 9-year-old Dorchester boy named Kenny Martin wandered into the station with a friend, Thomas Lydon. It was the day after Christmas and Kenny, who had come into Downtown Boston to buy some Boy Scout equipment, spent the afternoon horsing around with Lydon at the station. They’d chased each other up and down the escalators, running through the crowd of postholiday shoppers. As the afternoon came to an end, Lydon departed, while Kenny planned to take the train back home.

In his brown-checked jacket with fur collar, blue bell-bottom pants, and orange work boots, Kenny was a typical Dorchester boy, coming home from a day of fun. He was the youngest of four children, small for his age at less than 50 pounds. It might seem odd for a boy so young to be alone in the city, but Boston kids learned to use the subways early in those days. They often traveled on their own from one side of the city to the other.

The platform where he would’ve waited for the Dorchester train was cold and drafty, for there are few places colder than a Boston subway platform in late December. One could only stand and shiver, waiting for the sound of a faraway bell to warn people of approaching trains. Perhaps Kenny looked down the long, dark tunnel for the sign of a subway car’s light, usually visible long before the car was in the station. The tunnels were foreboding; there were stories of people accidentally getting electrocuted on the infamous “third rail” and of huge rodents living in the underground network. Meanwhile, pigeons, bats, and owls roosted in the rafters, occasionally swooping down to frighten the commuters.

There was no shortage of urban legends around South Station, of how people committed suicide by jumping in front of moving trains and how homeless men wandered in the dark tunnels to sleep underneath cardboard coverings. In time, stories of vagrants evolved into stories of trolls living in the tunnels, trolls who only came out after midnight when the station was closed. This was fantasy stuff, tales told by older kids to tease younger ones.

Of course, the station had its good points. It was a historical landmark, after all, opening for business in 1899 as the largest station in the country, a majestic building made of pink granite. There was also the railroad chapel, Our Lady of the Railways. Built in the 1950s, it was the first of its kind in America. Organ music played during every Sunday service, and Boston’s Archbishop Cushing held special masses and Easter vigils, perfect for travelers who couldn’t get home in time to worship. There was a lunch counter, a newsstand, the Sidecar Bar-Grill, a bakery, and a barbershop. A Paramount film crew had been to South Station earlier in the year to shoot a scene for a Jack Lemmon movie, The Out of Towners. For a few days, the dilapidated old station was enlivened by the buzz of Hollywood energy and curious crowds. Despite these occasional bright spots, the atmosphere remained glum and ramshackle. When the crowds thinned out after the rush hour, all that remained were boarded-up areas that always seemed to be “under construction” and weary cleaning crews wiping out the messes of the day.

At some point in the afternoon of December 26, Kenny met a pudgy, dark-haired man with a round face. The man seemed different from the other people hurrying around the station. He was rumpled. He needed a shave and a bath. It turned out the man was also named Kenneth. What they talked about, or how they spent their next few hours together, is unknown. History would reveal that the unshaven man knew all about the secret tunnels in South Station and knew all the special places where people could hide. He may have offered to show Kenny around the old building, an irresistible prospect for a 9-year-old boy.

Kenny’s body was found eleven days later. He’d been strangled to death. His body was hidden in one of the station’s underground passageways. Someone had wrapped it in a canvas bag and covered it with debris. A search team consisting of police from two districts, as well as city engineers, had spent the day exploring sewers and tunnels around the station. The search ended in an abandoned transit tunnel, a ghostly location that had once been used to transport cargo to the surface cars. It was a dingy place for a little boy to wind up, cold and dark and airless.

He could’ve been lured there only by one of the station’s trolls.

Security guards patrolled South Station and routinely tossed out vagrants and drunks, shoving them out the door onto Atlantic Avenue. These scenes were unpleasant, but the guards were under orders to keep the winos and grifters out. The raggedy station only looked worse if pitiful old drunks were lounging on the wooden benches. Yet Kenneth Harrison, the pudgy man, had been living in the place for nearly a year, like a hermit hiding in a cave. He didn’t have to compete for a bed at one of the nearby shelters, not when he could hunker down in one of the abandoned offices beneath the station.

The morning after he’d killed Kenny Martin, Harrison slouched out into the daylight, searching for a rooming house where he could find a bed and lie low. The sidewalk was still slippery from the previous night’s rain and sleet. It would have been a nice day to hang out at the station, yet Harrison felt it was time to go. Hanging around was too risky, even if the dead boy was buried deeper than an old bone.

Harrison had grown up in Roxbury’s Mission Hill neighborhood and had dropped out of school after the eighth grade. Now, at 31, he was an unemployed restaurant worker, living a vagabond’s existence and spending what little money he had on alcohol. He’d become one of life’s losers, a degenerate barfly with no future. He was virtually indistinguishable from dozens of others in his situation. The difference was that Harrison murdered children.

Kenny Martin, whose face would soon be featured in local newspapers, was Harrison’s second young victim. Two-and-a-half years earlier, Harrison had killed a 6-year-old girl named Lucy Palmarin. She’d been cashing in an empty tonic bottle at a store. Witnesses saw her climbing into the car of an unknown man. She was found floating among the garbage in South Boston’s Fort Point Channel, a mile from her home. Since the medical examiner found no signs of injury or foul play, Lucy’s death was ruled an accidental drowning. Lucy’s disappearance created a flurry of activity in South Boston. Posters with her picture were distributed throughout the community. Her poor mother waited up nights, clutching a book of old photographs of the missing girl. Three weeks into the search, the Boston police called in the FBI for assistance. They suspected a kidnapping, but the truth was worse.

On April 15, 1967, Harrison was driving a cab, among his many odd jobs. He would later tell a judge that he had dropped off a fare near the D Street housing project where Lucy lived. He saw her walking and offered to give her a ride. Instead of taking her home, he drove to the channel where he tossed her in the city’s notoriously dirty water.

In another version of the confession, Harrison said the little girl asked him for a quarter, which led to him giving her a piggyback ride. Once she was up on his back, he easily pitched her into the water. So he said. His confessions sounded ludicrous. Lucy’s family was Puerto Rican and new to America. The girl didn’t speak English. In between the two child murders, Harrison had killed two adults. There’d been a barroom beef with a fellow named Joseph Breen, an ex-marine and water company employee. Harrison and Breen had been drinking at the Novelty Bar in Boston’s Combat Zone, a dank neighborhood of nudie bars and X-rated theaters.

Later, after an argument over money, Harrison beat Breen to death with a rock.

Inexplicably, Harrison called the police that night, telling them they could find Breen’s body floating in an excavation pit on Kneeland Street near Chinatown. When the police asked who was calling, Harrison felt a laugh coming up his throat, like an eruption.

It was a time when killers were becoming celebrities, with memorable names and trademarks, like the Boston Strangler or the Zodiac in California. Why couldn’t Harrison be “The Giggler?”

Harrison must’ve felt as elusive as the Zodiac, because he’d actually returned to the Novelty a short time later. A couple of Breen’s friends were there and recognized him as the man who had been with Breen the night he was killed. Breen’s friends called the police, but by the time they arrived, Harrison was gone again, no doubt back at the train station, hiding in plain sight.

Then, just a month before killing Kenny Martin, Harrison had murdered an old woman, 75-year-old Clovis Parker of South Boston. As he’d done with the little girl, he left Clovis floating in Fort Point Channel, a mere five-minute walk from Harrison’s South Station hideout. He’d tell investigators that he had met the old woman on a bridge, and she’d asked for help getting across. Without giving a reason, Harrison said that he’d simply kicked Clovis Parker’s cane from under her and then tossed her over the guardrail. The unfortunate woman’s death hadn’t even made it to the newspapers.

A few days after killing Kenny Martin, Harrison called his sister, Eileen. He confessed that he had killed a boy and told her where the body was hidden. On January 6, the day Kenny’s body was found, Harrison boarded a train at South Station and left Boston.

Eileen consulted a lawyer and then called the police. They followed her tip to find the body, and then a quartet of detectives armed with an arrest warrant traced Harrison to Providence. They arrested him without incident and held him without bail in Suffolk County.

While detectives questioned him about Kenny Martin’s death, Harrison interrupted.

“As long as I’m here,” he said, “I might as well tell you about a few more.”

He told them about Lucy Palmarin, Joseph Breen, and Clovis Parker. Investigators were stunned. Harrison was confessing to four murders committed over a span of thirty-two months.

When he talked about Kenny Martin, Harrison said he’d had “an urge to kill” but didn’t remember doing anything. He merely woke up the next morning and saw the boy with a rope around his neck.

Harrison showed little emotion as he spoke, but he seemed comfortable talking about his crimes. He even took a liking to the detectives interrogating him. Later, when he learned that one of the detectives had retired, Harrison sent a card.

Yet his frankness about the murders and his friendship with the detectives masked a fragile mind.

Don Stradley is an award-winning journalist and author of several books. Boston Tabloid: The Killing of Robin Benedict (2022) was a top seller on Amazon Kindle and The War was a #1 seller in its category, praised in the Times of London, and selected as a Favorite of 2021 by The Progressive Magazine. His earlier titles Berserk (2019), A Fistful of Murder (2020), and Slaughter in the Streets (2020) focused on how the sport of boxing was touched by the world of crime. He has also written for various movie-streaming companies, including Fandor, The Film Detective, and Film Masters. He has appeared on several true crime podcasts.

#7684. Chimera

Rina Varger beat her palm against the old Ford pickup’s door in time to Aerosmith’s “Push Comes to Shove” as she drove across the bridge and into town. It was the morning of the tenth of September and the Merrimack was running high after a week of torrential rain, debris and dead brush from upriver borne along by the surging brown water. The wind in her face felt good after a day spent scrubbing years of dust and nameless gunk from between sticky floorboards. Everything had to be perfect for Aunt Eleanor’s wedding. Nana Marian was losing her mind trying to get the house in shape, running their skinless maid Kate Bartlett ragged.

A little after eight Rina parked in front of Julian and Eddie’s place, a cramped two-story bungalow with a patchy lawn and huge stands of sumac nearly obscuring its front entrance and encroaching on its drive-way. Julian, an aging queen cast off by a prominent Cape Cod family, owned Plover Antiques downtown. Eddie Means was a veterinarian at the Franklin Park Zoo in Boston, and had been the Varger family’s meat man for almost ten years. Rina killed the engine and stepped out onto the curb, fishing in her jacket pockets for her cigarettes. She was about to light up when she heard voices coming from the direction of the driveway. She pocketed her smokes and went around the house, moving slowly, keeping to the shadows of the sumac stand.

Four teenage boys, maybe fifteen or sixteen, and a girl who looked a little younger stood in a half circle at the end of the driveway, in front of Julian’s garage. Another girl, maybe a year or two older than the others, sat fenced in by their little gang with her back against the peeling garage door. Even from the curb, Rina could see the shiner discoloring her left eye and cheekbone. As she watched, one of the boys kicked the seated girl in the ribs. She gasped, bending double.

“Show us,” the biggest boy demanded. He was the whole pack-age, letter jacket and crew cut, neck and shoulders like a bull. “Come on, freak. Let’s see if it’s true.”

Rina bent and scooped up a stone from the lawn’s sandy edge, stepping out into the center of the driveway. She weighed the rock in her palm, sizing up the distance between her and the gang. Her mother would have stomped right into the middle of them, screaming that she’d call their parents. Her grandfather would have thrown his skin off then and there and gone for their throats. Her grandmother would have watched. “Somewhere down the middle,” Rina muttered to herself.

“I’ll do it myself,” said the boy. He knelt, a look of strange, compulsive hunger making him seem older than his years. The girl squeezed her eyes shut tight and pressed herself against the garage door. Rina took a deep breath, did her best Bruce Hurst windup, and threw the rock as hard as she could. The boy turned at her grunt of effort and took it square in the nose, his head snapping back like a speed bag. He went down on his ass with a shriek, clapping his hands over his gushing nose. Blood dripped into his lap as the others turned in shock. One went for a pocketknife.

Rina pulled her jacket back to show the revolver stuffed into the waist of her jeans. “Get lost,” she said. The gang stopped cold. She snapped her fingers. “Come on. Time’s a-wastin’.”

They remained frozen for a moment. One of the boys looked at their ringleader, then looked away, shamefaced and red. The girl in their little gang seemed on the verge of tears. Slowly, two of them helped the bleeding boy to his feet and led him past her toward the street. He glared at her in passing, poisonous hate and terror at war behind his beady blue eyes. “Fucking dyke,” he muttered.

“If I see you around here again, you’ll wish I hadn’t,” said Rina. “You got that, tiger?”

He ducked his head and ran, and the others ran after him, the girl looking back fearfully over her shoulder. When she was sure they were gone, Rina went to the girl sitting against the garage door and offered her a hand. She took it. “Thanks.” The girl got unsteadily to her feet, wiping dirt from her shirtfront. She was taller than Rina, chubby and a little stooped, with a round face and buck teeth. When she spoke, it was with the slightest lisp. “I’m Wendy.”

“Julian’s my uncle,” said Wendy, sniffing. “I’m staying with him for a little while.”

Wendy shook her head. “No. He’s okay.” She picked at the cuff of her sweatshirt. “I had, um, some problems with my mom. It’s why I’m out here.”

The side door banged open. Eddie hurried down the concrete steps, shirtless and barefoot in nothing but a pair of tan slacks. He wore a big buck knife on his hip. “You alright, honey?” he asked Wendy, though he didn’t for a moment look away from Rina. Rina smiled, showing all her teeth.

“That’s alright, then. Why don’t you go help your uncle with dinner?”

“Go on in, honey,” he said, firmly this time. Wendy took a hesitant step back, her cheeks reddening, and then fled inside.

“You stay away from that girl, Rina,” said Eddie. “She’s got enough problems.”

Eddie stuck his thumbs in his belt. He was only a few inches taller than Rina, and maybe thirty pounds heavier, but faggot or not, he wasn’t someone you wanted to fight. “Yes.”

Rina shrugged. She hadn’t really thought about Wendy like that, until Eddie told her not to. She tried on the idea of slipping her hands under that baggy sweatshirt, of tilting that soft, rounded chin up for a kiss, sweaty black hair tangled around her fingers. The things you weren’t supposed to eat were always the sweetest. “Fair enough,” she said, clearing her throat. “What you got for me?”

Eddie shook his head and went to lift the garage door. “Broad fucking daylight,” he said as the smell of ripe meat and preservatives billowed out around him in a fragrant cloud. Rina stepped closer, sniffing at the air. In the gloom of the garage, between rusted gym equipment and stacked cardboard boxes, the source of the smell lay wrapped in plastic on a dolly under a frayed blue tarp. Eddie looked back at her. “You may not care who sees you, but I lose my job and you’re gonna have to find someone else to play ball.”

Ignoring him, Rina went to the dolly and knelt, lifting the nearest corner of the tarp. A liquid black eye stared back at her through long, curling lashes. A dead Cape buffalo, maybe a year old, horns not yet fused over the crown of its skull. “Beautiful,” she said. She stood, letting the tarp fall back into place. “I’ll get the ramp.”

The things you weren’t supposed to eat were always the sweetest.

Rina took the back way home, the station crackling through the dead spots on the orchard road so that Captain and Tenille sounded like they were singing from the depths of a bottomless pit. She turned the radio off. She kept thinking of Wendy. Broken birds always got her going. Something about how vulnerable they were, how bad they needed someone to be good to them. Rina liked being that someone, at least at first. If you rode out the crying and the clinginess for a few weeks you could really put your feet up afterward. Coast on goodwill while they made you breakfast and ate you out on the couch.

“You’re just too bad.” She chuckled to herself, lighting a cigarette as she turned onto the old pumping station connector. Weighed down by the buffalo carcass in its bed, the truck thumped and rattled over the broken pavement where it gave way to dirt. The trees—old growth, not pine—crowded close so that their branches formed a tunnel of dappled shade over the road. Part of Rina always felt relief when she turned into that sheltering gloom, like she’d braved the open grasslands on a hunt and come back to the tribe with meat over her shoulder. Sometimes she envied those long-ago Skin Dancers their adventures, the danger they’d faced in a world not yet broken to the saddle.

A flock of wild turkeys darted into the road ahead of Rina. She slowed to let them cross, the tom keeping a wary eye on her as the hens hurried their half-grown pullets along. He was a big one, scarred on his head and neck and missing most of his comb. Not today, thought Rina, smiling at the tom. The fox in her itched and whined, pulling at her thoughts, turning them red and quick. She’d eaten it only a week before, and it still paced restlessly in her mind. You enjoy the weather, old man. We’ll Dance another time.

The big tom gobbled and fluffed his wings. The turkeys disappeared into the woods. Rina drove onward. She passed the burned-out wreck of the Mercer farm, half the big dairy barn still standing thirty-odd years after the fire that had killed three of the Mercers in their beds. Rina’s family owned the land now, but they’d never built on it. The Mercer cows had been sold off for dog food and the forest now crept step by careful step toward the blackened skeletons of the farmhouse and the barn. Rina remembered laying on her back beneath those sagging beams on her sixteenth birthday, bored and frustrated as Fabian La Vigne, her second cousin on Nana Marian’s side of the family, tentatively licked her pussy.

Rina wondered if Eleanor’s marriage would be like that. She’d never pictured Aunt Ellie with a man. Rina had a clear childhood memory of her aunt, maybe nineteen or twenty at the time, splashing in the shallows at Lake Winnisquam with some of their girl cousins from Memé Carlotte’s side of the family up in Maine, the Gerstmanns. Ellie, plump and long-legged in her two-piece, her red hair flying as she skimmed a palm across the surface of the water, droplets sparkling in the air, and that smile, alive with mischief and desire. Now she was marrying Rudy Gerstmann, her third cousin, a tall, soft-spoken man with a sandy mustache and the slender fingers of a pianist. Rina’s great-aunt Simone always said if you married outside the bloodline you’d wind up with chimeric babies, unable to control the Skin Dance. Her late uncle Cecil’s baby with the girl in town he’d fallen for had been stillborn, a patchwork horror of fur and feathers, but her uncle Albert’s bastard, Jean Paul, could Dance as well as any of them, and his mother was a diner waitress. When Rina asked Simone about that, her great-aunt told her it wasn’t decent to talk about matters of the bedroom.

Rina pulled onto Bear Lake Drive, the truck bouncing as it hit dirt road, the trees closing in tight to either side. A half mile in, Alfie Heureaux, one of her grandmother’s men and a distant cousin on the La Vigne side of the family, stood guard at the bottom of the driveway to Hensteeth, leaning against the rusted cattle gate, a lit cigarette dan-gling from his mouth. With his creased, leathery skin and colorless hair he might have been anywhere from fifty to seventy. He had a Dancing scar at the right corner of his mouth that pulled it down a little, and another at his hairline that gave him a little bald triangle above his right temple. He wore a weathered denim jacket over a plaid shirt.

“What’s the word, hummingbird?” he asked as Rina rolled to a stop beside his post, the Ford’s brakes squealing in protest.

“Not a thing, chicken wing,” Rina answered, smiling. “Anyone been down from the house?”

“Camille went out a little while ago.” Alfie blew smoke out his nostrils and inhaled it. He gestured with his cigarette at the tarped mass in the Ford’s bed. “Everything go okay with Siegfried and Roy there?”

“Fine, yeah,” said Rina. “You gonna make me fuckin’ sit here all day listening to you?”

Alfie shadowboxed at her, muttering good-naturedly, then chuckled and went to open the gate. The iron post dragged over the stony ground of the drive. He waved her in. “Someone’s gonna wash that mouth out with soap one of these days, kid,” he called after her.

It was a mile and a half through the woods to Hensteeth, the Varger family compound Rina’s great-grandparents had built at the dawn of the century. Manchester was a rich place then, textile factories booming on both sides of the river, lumber in the hills, distilleries pouring rivers of illegal booze south to Boston and Worcester, north to Concord and the seacoast. Great-grand-père Etienne and Great-grand-mère Antoinette built a mansion that made the governor’s residence at Bridges House look like a garden shed. Rina could see it through the trees, the four-story redbrick facade with its creeping ivy and its mullioned windows, the flash of light on the arboretum glass, and behind them the low bulk of the Old House built back against Thrush Hill, which rose two hundred feet of cut and blasted rock to a wooded ridge where deer sometimes passed by in single file.

Emil sat out in front of the garage in a rusty deck chair, his shotgun propped beside him, when Rina pulled into the circular driveway. He nodded at her. One of the cats, a big black queen, ran out of the bay and between his legs, a mouse in her jaws. She paused to look at Rina for a moment, then darted away into the gardens. Rina put the truck in park and tossed Emil the keys. Gravel crunched beneath her boots. “Make sure this gets to the kitchen,” she told him, jerking her thumb back at the truck’s bed. “Is anyone here yet?”

“Not yet,” he said, shifting his toothpick from one corner of his mouth to the other as he stood. He was tall and very thin, his hair pomaded, his coat fashionable. Emil was Great-aunt Adeline and Great-uncle Louis’s eldest, a distant cousin on the Cotard side of the family, Rina’s great-grand-mère Antoinette’s kin; he’d come down from Quebec just the year before. “They are come later. Ce soir.”

Rina left him to take the Ford around the back of the house. For a while she walked through the gardens, which were thinning out as fall came on, the lilacs long since gone, the pink crab apple blossoms trodden to fragrant, oily humus. She stopped for a while by the piscine, watching the carp swim in the dark green water in the shade of a line of cypress, the morning sky reflected in the surface. She thought about Wendy again. Julian’s niece wasn’t bad-looking. Rina liked a little something to grab on to, even if Wendy was only a kid . . .

Don’t make a problem where there isn’t one, she told herself. She flicked her cigarette butt into the water. A fish swam up to investigate it, then turned and dove. Across the pool, a peacock strutted over mossy stones, its tail feathers dragging in the dust.

On her way to the house, Rina came across her grandmother bedding down the rose bushes, patting mulch over their roots with her long, gnarled hands. Marian Varger was a big woman, two hundred pounds or more, and almost six feet tall. Since Grand-père Henry’s second stroke in ’63 she’d kept the family’s interests in line. The gambling, the loan sharking, the hijacking rings and protection rackets. The first unions in Manchester to try holding back the payments they’d owed her husband had learned the hard way not to cross her. Her Dancing scars must have helped put the fear of God in those hard old New Englanders. Her large, square face looked to have been cut apart and glued together without much regard for symmetry. Her right eye, black and piercing, was a full inch higher than her drooping, milky left, and her nose had been broken several times and flattened slightly on its left side. When she smiled, which wasn’t often, the scars that crisscrossed her lips pulled her face into a grotesque, leering grimace, her gums and teeth showing like a horse’s.

Marian saw Rina and rose, wiping her hands on her apron. They embraced and kissed each other on both cheeks. Marian broke away and held Rina at arm’s length. “Lunch is in an hour,” she said. “Wash up, and change into something decent. You look like a hood.”

“Get,” said Marian, not unkindly, and sent Rina on her way with a swat across the backside. Rina jogged the rest of the way to the house. She was excited for the wedding. Her mother would be a wreck over it, but what else was new? Marguerite had never really been all there. Rina saw other mothers with their kids in town, holding their hands on the street, carrying them in slings and backpacks, rubbing noses and kissing. Playing in the park. All her childhood memories were of her grandmother, or her great-aunt Celene, or Aunt Ellie. She remembered her uncle Harry a little bit from before he’d left. A big smile. Thick black hair. He’d used to give her shoulder rides across the lawn. No one had seen him in twenty years.

Her uncle Albert lay dozing on the landing in the skin of a tiger, watching her with half-closed eyes as she climbed the stairs. The sharp, musky smell of him hung in the air like gasoline fumes.

The house’s foyer was empty, the dark wood of the branching front staircase leading up to the second floor gleaming in the light that came in through the oculus. Kate the maid lurked just to the left of it, dusting a vase with morose intensity. Beyond the landing’s big mullioned windows, the courtyard garden’s old willow swayed in a gentle breeze. Rina took off her boots by the door and crossed the Oriental carpet barefoot, running her palm over the worn brow of the stone lion at the center of the room for luck as she passed by. Her uncle Albert lay dozing on the landing in the skin of a tiger, watching her with half-closed eyes as she climbed the stairs. The sharp, musky smell of him hung in the air like gasoline fumes. His tail, hanging between the handrail’s slats, twitched slowly back and forth.

The third-story hall was silent, but as Rina passed the door to her mother’s room she heard the groan of something heavy moving across the floor. She paused. Kneeling, she looked through the keyhole and into the dimly lit room. Within, Marguerite lay naked on her bed. The curtains were drawn and the late morning sunlight shone through them, weak and reddish. At the foot of the bed, a polar bear stood on its hind legs, towering nearly to the ceiling. Rina watched through the keyhole as the bear approached her mother. She could smell its carrion breath and the oily reek of its yellow-white pelt. It rested one tremendous paw on Marguerite’s leg, its claws dimpling her flesh. It nosed her heavy thighs apart, chuffing softly, and Rina saw a flash of rough pink tongue between her mother’s legs.

“Careful,” Marguerite whispered. “Careful, darling.” Slowly, she wrapped her thighs around the bear’s huge skull. It retreated half a step, dragging her toward the end of her bed, her long auburn hair trailing over the sheets. She let out a squeal of delight and Rina turned away and straightened, her face burning. What did you expect, pervert? She backed up from the door, walking on tiptoe as the sounds from behind it grew quicker and more frenzied. She didn’t know who was with her mother. She didn’t want to.

Rina’s room was the last on the right, its single dormer window looking out over the north lawn and the ridge and the Old House built up flush to the rock face. She flopped down on her narrow twin bed, staring up at her poster of Gene Simmons onstage at the band’s 1977 Madison Square Garden show, his face a grinning death mask, his bare arms slick with sweat. You could tell from the way the tendons in his wrist and on the back of his picking hand stood out that he was really going for it. Balls out. Rina sighed and slipped her hand down the front of her pants. Her skin was hot. Dampness met her fingers.

She’d just jerk off a little, just to come, and to get Wendy out of her head. Blow out the bad vibes from seeing her mother with whoever she was fucking these days. That was all. She closed her eyes, getting to work. Her breath came a little faster.

#7683. Judge halts CFPB firings

In the same order, the bureau was told not to delete any agency data or transfer its reserve funding to the Fed or anywhere else. The CFPB then reportedly placed most workers on administrative leave.

A federal judge has ordered the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its acting director, Russ Vought, not to terminate any agency employee except for cause related to job performance or conduct until March 3, when another hearing in the case will take place.

The bureau responded, however, by placing on administrative leave all employees except those asked to return to work by “the Acting Director, Chief Legal Officer, or another designee,” according to an email from the CFPB’s human capital operations manager that was seen by Bloomberg Law.

The court order on Friday came after the National Treasury Employees Union urged Judge Amy Berman Jackson on Thursday to block Vought from a “mass firing” it believed would affect 95% of the bureau’s workforce as early as Friday.

In the same Friday order, Berman Jackson demanded that the CFPB “not delete, destroy, remove, or impair” any data or agency records covered by the Federal Records Act.

Berman Jackson also ordered the CFPB and Vought not to transfer money from the bureau's reserve funds, other than "to satisfy” the agency’s “ordinary operating obligations.” That includes returning money from the CFPB’s reserve funds to the Federal Reserve, as Vought said this month he would do.

The data-related developments follow a declaration the CFPB’s former chief technologist, Erie Meyer, filed with the court Friday, warning that databases holding 12 years’ worth of information the agency has collected would soon be deleted and “irretrievably lost.”

Affected data would include “supervisory and examination records of financial institutions, enforcement action data, consumer complaints, personal consumer information, and market research records,” Meyer wrote.

Loss of data that tracks institutions’ financial behavior “would impair the Bureau's ability to identify risks and respond to emerging threats within the financial system,” Meyer wrote.

“This could destabilize markets, allow bad actors to exploit weaknesses in financial institutions, and undermine public trust in the financial system,” she wrote.

It would also open the financial system to market manipulation, Meyer asserted.

“Tech companies moving into financial services could gain an illegal competitive advantage by accessing sensitive consumer financial data or enforcement records, and the audit logs of that activity could be deleted,” she wrote. “This could result in unfair competition and undermine market integrity.”

That may serve as a reference to X Money, the payments tool set for launch this year in a partnership between card network Visa and social media platform X, owned by Trump adviser Elon Musk, who’s also seen as the architect behind the Department of Government Efficiency, which infiltrated the CFPB this month.

The deletion of CFPB data “would leave consumers without critical recourse in the event of financial harm caused by institutions under the Bureau's jurisdiction,” Meyer wrote. Further, she asserted, it would make the CFPB’s Consumer Response database “unavailable and/or unreliable, severely hamper — if not entirely take down — the Bureau’s website, and likely result in the loss of mandatory public reporting the Bureau has previously done.”

Friday’s order may represent a relief to CFPB employees, but it doesn’t apply to bureau employees who have already been terminated. The agency last Tuesday terminated roughly 70 probationary employees, then Thursday fired another 70 to 100 term employees – those whose contracts have set limits between one and four years.

Altogether, last week’s firings cut roughly 10% of the CFPB's workforce, according to American Banker.

The CFPB was not the only banking regulator to see workforce reductions last week. Roughly 500 employees at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., or about 8% of its workforce, accepted a deferred resignation offer from the Trump administration, Bloomberg Law reported Friday, citing a spokesperson for the agency.

The FDIC then terminated probationary employees, the outlet reported Monday, though the number of employees affected remained unclear.

An FDIC spokesperson on Friday did not detail how deeply certain units of the regulator were affected.

A lawyer representing the CFPB workers’ union laid out the urgency of Friday’s court action.

”I’m asking that they don't fire the entire agency tonight,” Deepak Gupta, a founding principal at Gupta Wessler, told the court, according to American Banker. “I don’t want to leave the courthouse without some assurance that the mass layoff is not going to happen and then become a fait accompli.”

The workers’ union asked Thursday for a temporary restraining order to stop the firings, but agreed to seek a preliminary injunction instead.

That mirrors a case in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, in which the city of Baltimore sued the CFPB, claiming Vought’s move to return the agency’s funding to the Fed would effectively shut down the bureau “by fiat.”

The government agreed Thursday that Vought would refrain from transferring money out of the CFPB’s reserve fund or returning money to the Fed or Treasury until Feb. 28, or upon a “contrary order” from the court, Bloomberg Law reported.

Still, in the workers’ union case, Brad Rosenberg, a Justice Department special counsel, objected to the request for a preliminary injunction.

"We don't think any preliminary relief is appropriate at this stage because we don't think the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits," he said, according to American Banker.

Among the employees the CFPB terminated Thursday is Julia Barnard, who served as the agency’s student loan ombudsman since last February. Her position is mandated by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.

“This work matters,” Barnard said in a statement issued by the Student Borrower Protection Center. “It’s a lifeline for borrowers and a safeguard against a system that too often fails them. Dismantling this function is unconscionable and will cost real people real money.”

Delaying any further moves to slash the CFPB workforce would at least give employees time to plan and budget for their personal futures. Employees of the agency are entitled by law to 60 days’ notice of job loss. But last week’s firings came with no notice and with immediate effect.

Further, terminations for cause (probationary employees, for example, were notified that they were deemed “not fit for continued employment because [their] ability, knowledge and skills do not fit the Agency’s current needs”) left those employees without access to severance, one lawyer with the CFPB told ABC News.

In Vought’s first week as the CFPB’s acting director, the bureau’s headquarters were closed to employees, who were ordered to stop all bureau work. A tip line was also set up for people to report on employees who might be conducting work.

#7681. Judicial Watch founder Larry Klayman disbarred by Supreme Court

The U.S. Supreme Court disbarred conservative watchdog group Judicial Watch founder and activist Larry Klayman on Monday following his 18-month suspension issued last year by the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. (Image from Shutterstock)

The U.S. Supreme Court disbarred conservative watchdog group Judicial Watch founder and activist Larry Klayman on Monday following his 18-month suspension issued last year by the District of Columbia Court of Appeals.

Klayman’s disbarment follows a suspension for violating numerous ethical rules in connection to representing rancher Cliven Bundy in Nevada federal court, Law360 reports.

Bundy had been facing a criminal case over his 2014 standoff with federal agents when Klayman, a Florida attorney, sought pro hac vice status to join Bundy’s legal team in 2016. The District of Columbia Office of Disciplinary Counsel filed a complaint against Klayman in 2018, claiming that he misled the U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada about his disciplinary status when he tried to represent Bundy. A D.C. appellate court ruling adopted the District of Columbia Bar’s findings and suspension.

The disciplinary office alleged that Klayman also made baseless claims against the judge who denied his admission to the Nevada court.

Klayman, in a statement to Law360 on Monday said, “The order contains no factual or legal reasoning, is subject to reconsideration and is not final. I made a compelling submission to the Supreme Court recently, and apparently, it was not considered. This will be a basis for reconsideration.”

#7679. Who Is Elena Kagan? Ideology, strategy, and the art of disagreement

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On May 21, 2026, Justice Elena Kagan did something she had never done in nearly 16 years on the Supreme Court: she dissented alone in a signed decision. The case, Havana Docks v. Royal Caribbean Cruises, concerned whether cruise lines could face liability for using Cuban docks confiscated decades earlier. Eight justices, including Kagan’s liberal colleagues Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson, sided against the cruise lines. Kagan thought the majority had misunderstood a basic principle of property law: the interest originally confiscated had expired long before the cruise ships arrived.

The solitary dissent was unusual for a justice who has spent much of her tenure avoiding separate opinions. At a judicial conference in July 2025, Kagan observed that the court “speaks best when it speaks as a court,” and acknowledged that she sometimes drafts dissents only to decide against publishing them.

Kagan’s professional background is also unusual. She is the only current justice who arrived at the Supreme Court without previously serving as a judge. Before her appointment in 2010, she had been a law professor, dean of Harvard Law School, a White House adviser, and solicitor general of the United States. Her career was therefore shaped substantially by institutions in which persuasion, negotiation, and managing competing perspectives are routine.

But how much does this explain her jurisprudence? Ideological measures generally place Kagan to the right of her liberal colleagues, and her voting record contains meaningful differences from Sotomayor’s and Jackson’s. Yet those differences are far from uniform, and Kagan’s reluctance to write separately persists even when she reaches precisely the same result as her colleagues.

Understanding Kagan therefore requires examining not only how she votes, but how she chooses to agree and disagree.

Kagan has generally occupied a position to the right of the other liberal justices in measures of Supreme Court ideology. But the distance between them depends considerably on how ideology is measured, which cases are examined, and when the comparison is made.

The best-known measure is the Martin–Quinn score, which estimates the justices’ ideological positions from their voting patterns over time. In the 2024-25 term, Kagan’s score was −1.85, compared with −2.80 for Jackson and −4.19 for Sotomayor. Kagan was thus the rightmost of the three liberals, although she remained substantially to the left of the court’s median justice, Amy Coney Barrett, whose score was +0.53. The estimates for Jackson and Kagan had been closer in earlier terms (and, in fact, Jackson was initially positioned slightly to Kagan’s right).

The scores capture something revealing about how the justices vote, but they do not directly measure the substance of their legal reasoning or their willingness to compromise. Nor does a justice’s location relative to the other liberals necessarily reveal whether her own jurisprudence has changed. Martin–Quinn estimates are relative positions derived from voting coalitions, and those coalitions are themselves influenced by the court’s membership and docket.

The voting record offers a more concrete comparison. During the 2010–2021 terms, there were 56 contested decisions in which Kagan joined the majority while Sotomayor dissented, compared with just 19 in which their positions were reversed. Kagan was nearly three times as likely to be on the prevailing side when the two disagreed. That is a substantial difference, although it does not establish that every disagreement reflected an ideological division.

Justice Stephen Breyer, long considered a moderate liberal on the court, provides a useful point of reference. During their overlapping time on the court, Kagan joined the majority without Breyer 41 times, while Breyer joined the majority without Kagan 31 times. The more balanced relationship suggests that Kagan’s historical voting behavior often resembled Breyer’s more closely than Sotomayor’s.

The picture has changed since Jackson joined the court in 2022. Across 121 contested decisions in which Kagan and Sotomayor both participated through the 2025 term, they voted on the same side 109 times. Kagan prevailed without Sotomayor seven times, while Sotomayor prevailed without Kagan five times. Their historical difference in majority participation has thus narrowed dramatically.

The convergence is particularly visible in closely divided cases. Of 82 decisions decided 5–4 or 6–3 in which Kagan, Sotomayor, and Jackson all participated, the three liberals voted together in 71. When the court divided most sharply, Kagan usually found herself alongside her liberal colleagues rather than occupying a position between the liberal and conservative wings.

There are then two different stories in the numbers. Over much of her tenure, Kagan was more likely than Sotomayor to support outcomes favored by conservative justices. More recently, that distinction has diminished, particularly in closely divided cases. Whether this reflects a change in Kagan’s jurisprudence or the changing opportunities for cross-ideological agreement remains uncertain.

The cases in which she breaks with her liberal colleagues offer a way to examine that distinction more closely.

One way to identify a comparatively moderate justice is to examine how frequently she votes with colleagues across the ideological divide. By that measure, Kagan has demonstrated considerable independence from her liberal colleagues.

Across 26 terms, Kagan was the only liberal voting alongside conservative justices in 27 contested decisions, approximately 5.3% of her non-unanimous votes. Sotomayor occupied that position in 18 decisions, or 3.4%. Yet Breyer did so in 29 cases, representing 7.1% of his contested votes during the years he served alongside Kagan. When he was on the court, Breyer, rather than Kagan, was more likely to separate from the other liberals in that way.

The pattern becomes even more interesting with Jackson’s arrival. During the 2022–2025 terms, Kagan was the sole liberal voting with conservatives in nine contested cases, compared with ten for Jackson (though this frequency has decreased) and just two for Sotomayor. Jackson’s cross-ideological votes were evenly divided between joining majorities and dissents, while Kagan’s predominantly placed her in the majority. Thus, even when two justices cross ideological lines with similar frequency, they may not be doing the same thing.

These voting coalitions also raise a question about Kagan’s reputation as a consensus-builder. Does she actually attract more conservative support when writing for the court?

The analysis provides surprisingly little evidence that she does. Of Kagan’s 47 majority opinions in contested decisions, 27 attracted at least three conservative votes. Sotomayor achieved the same result in 30 of her 49 contested majority opinions. Their records are then similar, suggesting that Kagan’s reputation for building agreement is not necessarily reflected in a distinctive ability to assemble ideologically diverse majorities.

The individual cases also complicate the idea that Kagan’s departures from the liberal wing are simply strategic compromises. In 2020’s Kahler v. Kansas, for example, Kagan wrote for six justices, including five conservatives, holding that the Constitution does not require states to recognize an insanity defense based on a defendant’s inability to distinguish right from wrong. Breyer, joined by Ginsburg and Sotomayor, dissented. Kagan emphasized the historical diversity of insanity rules and the latitude afforded to state legislatures; Breyer saw Kansas’s approach as eliminating a fundamental protection deeply rooted in criminal law.

Four years later, Pulsifer v. United States presented a dispute over the meaning of a single conjunction in a federal sentencing statute. Kagan wrote for a six-justice majority, including five conservatives, adopting a reading that restricted defendants’ eligibility for relief from mandatory minimum sentences. Gorsuch dissented, joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, favoring an interpretation that would have made relief more widely available.

Neither case is easily explained as Kagan merely accommodating conservative colleagues and both show substantive disagreements over the meaning of legal rules, with significant consequences for criminal defendants.

These decisions also show why ideological distance and judicial method cannot be treated as interchangeable. Kagan’s cross-ideological votes sometimes reflect legal commitments that produce outcomes different from those favored by her liberal colleagues. They also suggest that her willingness to build agreement does not automatically lead her toward the narrowest available resolution.

If Kagan is not consistently more successful than Sotomayor at attracting conservative votes, the more distinctive feature of her jurisprudence may lie elsewhere: what she does after reaching agreement, and particularly when she decides that a disagreement warrants an opinion of her own.

The art of agreement: choosing when to write

The most distinctive feature of Kagan’s judicial behavior may have less to do with how she votes than with how she expresses agreement. During her 16 terms on the court, Kagan authored just 18 concurrences in signed decisions, compared with 81 for Sotomayor. Breyer, often described as an institutionally minded pragmatist, also wrote concurrences at more than twice Kagan’s rate during their overlapping service. Jackson has been considerably more prolific in her shorter tenure. Kagan’s comparative restraint is therefore striking even among justices who share many of her substantive positions.

The difference becomes even more revealing when the comparison is limited to cases in which the justices reached exactly the same outcome. Between 2010 and 2021, Kagan and Sotomayor both supported a conservative-authored majority opinion in 93 contested decisions. Sotomayor wrote separately in 13 of those cases; Kagan did so in just one. The difference is difficult to explain through ideology or case selection alone: the two justices were participating in the same decisions, agreeing with the same majorities, yet approaching the question of whether to write separately very differently.

The distinction has narrowed somewhat in recent years, but it has not vanished. During the 2022–2025 terms, Kagan wrote separately in three of 38 conservative-authored majorities she shared with Sotomayor, compared with five for Sotomayor. In 29 comparable cases involving Kagan and Jackson, Kagan wrote separately twice and Jackson eight times. These samples are smaller, but they reinforce the larger finding that Kagan is particularly reluctant to add her individual voice to an outcome she already supports.

Kagan herself has offered a remarkably candid explanation for this. Speaking at the 9th Circuit Judicial Conference in July 2025, she described the Supreme Court as an institution whose opinions should communicate a collective judgment. She acknowledged that producing a single institutional voice requires “a little bit of flexibility and compromise.” Separate opinions, she suggested, can complicate the law by presenting competing explanations of what the court has supposedly decided.

Yet Kagan’s restraint should not be mistaken for unqualified agreement. In 2024’s United States v. Rahimi, she joined Roberts’ majority upholding a federal restriction on firearm possession by individuals subject to certain domestic violence restraining orders. She also joined Sotomayor’s concurrence, which defended the majority’s application of New York State Rifle & Pistol Association Inc. v. Bruen while reiterating their disagreement with that earlier Second Amendment decision holding there to be a constitutional right to carry a firearm. Jackson wrote her own concurrence addressing the difficulties lower courts had encountered applying Bruen. All three liberals agreed with the outcome, but their choices about authorship differed.

A similar pattern appeared in 2023’s National Pork Producers Council v. Ross, in which the court rejected an argument by pork producers that a law violated the Constitution by regulating the pork industry outside of California. Kagan joined Sotomayor’s separate opinion explaining why they agreed with the judgment without embracing portions of Gorsuch’s reasoning that threatened to alter the established constitutional framework. Kagan was willing to register a qualification, but she did so by joining a colleague’s opinion rather than writing another.

These distinctions again complicate the portrayal of Kagan as a consensus-builder. The data do not show that she consistently attracts more conservative support to her own majority opinions than Sotomayor does. They show something different: Kagan is considerably more selective about articulating separate disagreements when she already supports the court’s disposition. That behavior may preserve a clearer institutional message, but it also leaves fewer public indication of her reservations about particular decisions.

The difference matters when interpreting Kagan’s ideological position. A justice who joins an opinion without writing separately may appear closer to its author than one who publishes a concurrence, even when both share the same substantive objection. Kagan’s record suggests the absence of a separate opinion can reflect a decision about judicial expression rather than any lack of disagreement.

The limits of agreement: textualism, precedent, and dissent

Kagan’s willingness to work across ideological lines has never meant avoiding deep disagreements with the court’s conservatives. Some of her sharpest opinions have challenged not only their conclusions but also their fidelity to the interpretive principles they profess to follow.

In a 2015 lecture at Harvard Law School honoring Antonin Scalia, Kagan famously remarked, “We’re all textualists now.” The observation acknowledged Scalia’s influence on statutory interpretation, including among justices who did not share his ideological commitments. Seven years later, in her dissent in West Virginia v. EPA, Kagan explicitly revisited that statement: “It seems I was wrong.”

Her objection concerned the majority’s use of the major questions doctrine to restrict the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority under the Clean Air Act. Kagan argued that the court had departed from ordinary statutory interpretation by demanding an unusually clear congressional authorization for agency action of substantial economic or political significance. In her account, the conservative majority’s claimed commitment to textualism yielded when the statutory text pointed toward an outcome it disfavored.

The exchange is revealing because Kagan was challenging the majority from within a methodology often associated with conservative jurisprudence. Her embrace of textualism did not entail agreement with the conservatives about what particular statutes meant, much less about how much authority courts should exercise over Congress and administrative agencies.

That distinction became even clearer in 2024’s Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. Writing for the three liberals, subject to Jackson’s recusal in one of the consolidated cases, Kagan defended Chevron deference (deferring to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes) against the majority’s decision to overrule it. Her argument rested on statutory interpretation, congressional allocation of authority, administrative expertise, and the importance of precedent (a common theme for her). Textualism, in Kagan’s jurisprudence, does not necessarily require courts to resolve every statutory ambiguity without deference to an agency authorized to administer the law.

The same institutional concerns appear in her criticism of the court’s emergency docket. In Trump v. Wilcox, Kagan dissented from an order permitting the administration, pending further litigation, to remove officials from independent agencies. Joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, she objected both to the treatment of longstanding precedent and to the use of an expedited proceeding to alter the practical operation of existing law without ordinary briefing and argument.

These opinions provide an important counterweight to Kagan’s reputation for accommodation. Her restraint in writing separately does not preclude forceful disagreement when she believes the court has departed from established interpretive or institutional principles. Nor does that pattern necessarily distinguish her substantive positions from those of Sotomayor and Jackson, who joined these dissents.

The recurring question is therefore not simply whether Kagan is willing to compromise but where she draws the line between disagreements she can accommodate and those that she considers important enough to articulate publicly.

Sixteen years of decisions reveal a justice whose reputation for moderation captures only part of her judicial behavior. Kagan has historically been more willing than Sotomayor to join conservative-supported outcomes, and some of those differences reflect genuine disagreements about the law. Yet the gap has narrowed considerably in recent terms, particularly in cases that divide the court along ideological lines.

What distinguishes Kagan more consistently is her approach to disagreement. She is not uniquely successful at attracting conservative votes to her majority opinions. Rather, she is unusually reluctant to write separately when she can support an existing opinion, even in cases where her liberal colleagues reach the same result but feel compelled to explain their reservations. Her willingness to join another justice’s concurrence further complicates any assumption that silence necessarily signifies agreement.

The distinction has become more consequential as the court has moved rightward. Kagan’s opportunities to assemble majorities across ideological lines have diminished, while her dissents in disputes over administrative authority, precedent, and institutional power have become an increasingly public part of her jurisprudence.

Whether those patterns reflect a conscious strategy, enduring professional instincts, or some combination of the two cannot be determined from voting records alone. But the comparisons suggest that understanding Kagan requires looking beyond where she falls on an ideological scale. Her place on the court is defined both by the legal positions she takes and by the choices she makes about when – and how – to express them.

Dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

#7676. Federal judge sides with Biden Labor Dept. on ESG fiduciary rule

A Texas Northern District Court judge said the rule is still valid under Loper Bright and does not violate the Employment Retirement Income Security Act of 1974.

The Labor Department rule in question, “Prudence and Loyalty in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights,” was finalized in 2022 and has been in effect since January 2023. The rule was designed to overturn guidance the agency issued in 2020 under the first Trump administration that forbade fiduciaries from utilizing “non-pecuniary” factors in investment decisions.

The 2022 rule was designed to overturn a “chilling effect” that the Biden administration’s Labor Department said was witnessed under the 2020 rule. The guidance revised the agency’s tiebreaker standard to allow for consideration of collateral benefits like ESG in the event that two or more investments would equally serve the plan’s best interests but it would be imprudent to invest in both or all options.

The DOL rule has been repeatedly challenged by a coalition of 26 Republican-led states, who argued it runs afoul of ERISA and exceeded the agency’s statutory authority. However, Kacsmaryk disagreed in his Feb. 14 ruling and said such a reading of the law “embodies the wooden textualism that courts should endeavor to avoid.”

“Under the rule, a fiduciary faced with choosing between investment options — that all equally serve the beneficiaries' financial interests — does not advance the interests of nonbeneficiaries nor act for a purpose other than their financial benefit when he chooses based on collateral factors,” the judge ruled. “Plaintiffs' interpretation of ERISA would demand arbitrary randomness to choose between such investment options.”

The Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo case — which determined the fate of the Chevron doctrine — was decided in the time between Kacsmaryk’s initial dismissal of the case and when the plaintiffs and the Biden administration’s Labor Department argued before the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Supreme Court’s decision in June 2024 overturned the Chevron doctrine, which previously directed courts to give agencies deference in their interpretations of ambiguous law statutes.

While the parties had opposing views on how Chevron’s demise affected the case at hand, the Fifth Circuit refused to rule on the case, but vacated the initial dismissal and asked Kacsmaryk whether the rule can be squared with ERISA or the Administrative Procedure Act in light of Loper Bright.

Kacsmaryk said Loper Bright “did not disturb how courts evaluate a rule under the APA's arbitrary and capricious standard,” in his ruling Friday. He said the overturn of the Chevron doctrine should change how courts should interpret statutes, but not how they review the reasonableness of agency decisions.

The judge said that the tiebreaker standard in the 2022 rule does not violate ERISA’s duty of loyalty nor its requirement that fiduciaries act “solely” and for the “exclusive” benefit of the plan’s financial interests. Kacsmaryk said ERISA defines “whose interest the fiduciary must protect” and what their purpose is, but “says nothing of what they may consider.”

“Just as a driver, duty-bound to choose the fastest route to his destination, may choose the most scenic of two routes that each bring him to his destination at the same time, so too can a fiduciary choose a preferable investment option between two that will equally satisfy his duty of loyalty,” the judge wrote.

The coalition of Republican-led states were also joined in their lawsuit by public oilfield services company Liberty Energy, where Energy Secretary Chris Wright served as CEO at the time. The plaintiffs have previously signaled a willingness to fight the case all the way to the Supreme Court, but first it will return to the Fifth Circuit panel that initially heard the arguments.

However, it remains to be seen how the Trump administration’s Labor Department will handle the case. Experts have previously expressed concerns about the DOL’s rule being one of the Biden administration’s ESG-related regulations likely to be put on the chopping block under Trump.
